Read your estimated one-rep max and the training loads at each percentage.
guide.explanationTitle: How a one-rep max is estimated
guide.formula: Epley: 1RM = weight × (1 + reps ÷ 30)
explanation: A one-rep max is the heaviest weight you can lift once with good form, and it anchors most strength programming. Testing it directly demands a long warm-up and carries injury risk, so in practice it is estimated from a set of multiple reps. The widely used Epley formula assumes each additional rep corresponds to roughly 3.33% less weight, which is one thirtieth.

Other formulas such as Brzycki, Lombardi and O'Conner agree closely between 1 and 10 reps, usually within 2% to 5%, but accuracy collapses beyond about 10 reps because endurance, lactate tolerance and conditioning start to dominate rather than pure strength. Base your estimate on a set of 2 to 10 reps. Remember too that the result is a programming reference, not a competition number: your true max on a given day depends heavily on fatigue, technique and how thoroughly you warmed up.
guide.tableTitle: Formula comparison (bench press 80 kg × 5)

faq.q: Can I just attempt the estimated max?
faq.a: Not recommended, especially if you are relatively new to training. Estimates can sit 5% to 10% away from your true max, so going straight for the number carries real risk. A safer route is to test 90% of the estimate, confirm the technique holds, then add 2.5 to 5 kg per attempt until form breaks, always with a spotter or safety bars.

faq.q: Why does the estimate get worse with more reps?
faq.a: Because the limiting factor changes. Sets of 1 to 5 reps reflect maximal strength, but beyond roughly 10 to 12 reps, muscular endurance, lactate tolerance and conditioning take over, and those are not a linear extension of pure strength. Every formula therefore states a valid range, usually 2 to 10 reps, and results distort badly outside it.

faq.q: How should I set training loads from a 1RM percentage?
faq.a: A common structure is 85% to 100% for 1 to 5 reps for strength, 65% to 80% for 6 to 12 reps for hypertrophy, and 60% to 70% for 15 to 20 reps for endurance. Beginners do well starting at 60% to 70% while they groove technique, then raising intensity gradually. Exact percentages shift with training age and recovery capacity.

faq.q: What is a normal ratio between lifts?
faq.a: Individual variation is large, but rough benchmarks for trained lifters are a squat around 1.5 times bodyweight, a bench around 1.0 times and a deadlift around 1.75 to 2.0 times. Female lifters typically reach about 60% to 70% of the numbers of a male of the same bodyweight, largely because of differences in muscle distribution and hormones. Treat these as context, not targets.

pace-calculator.name: Pace
pace-calculator.description: Calculate running pace, speed, and race times
pace-calculator.metaDescription: Calculate your running pace, predict race times, and plan your training

steps: Choose: distance+time → pace, or pace+distance → finish time.
Enter distance (m/km/mi) and time, or your target pace.
See pace (min:sec per km), finish time, and split suggestions.
guide.formula: pace = time ÷ distance; time = pace × distance
explanation: Pace is time per unit distance, shown as 'min:sec per km'. It's the yardstick of training intensity: at the same heart rate, slower pace means lower intensity.
Deriving pace from distance+time tells if a run met its goal; pace+distance previews finish time for race or training planning.
Switch metric/imperial to turn a goal like 'sub-30 5K' into a daily executable pace range.

faq.q: Pace vs speed?
faq.a: Speed is distance per time (12 km/h); pace is time per distance (5:00/km). Runners use pace because it maps to 'how hard each km feels'.

faq.q: How to plan training with pace?
faq.a: Use easy/tempo/interval pace zones. After this tool gives target pace, fine-tune by heart rate or feel.

faq.q: Calculated time far from actual?
faq.a: Terrain, wind, fatigue slow you. Pace is the ideal-flat reference; add margin for hills or headwind.

macro-calculator.name: Macro
macro-calculator.metaDescription: Calculate your optimal protein, carbs, and fat intake for your fitness goals

steps: Enter sex, age, height and weight so the basal metabolic rate can be calculated.
Choose your activity level and goal, whether fat loss, maintenance or muscle gain, to set the calorie target.
Read the gram splits for protein, carbohydrate and fat, and adjust carbs and fats to taste.
guide.formula: Protein g = weight kg × factor; fat g = calories × fat share ÷ 9; carbs g = remaining ÷ 4
explanation: Macronutrients differ in energy density: protein and carbohydrate provide about 4 kcal per gram, fat about 9, and alcohol about 7. The usual order is to set protein first, then fat, and let carbohydrate fill the remainder. The reason is that protein and fat have minimum requirements, protein for muscle retention and satiety, fat for hormone production and absorption of fat-soluble vitamins, while carbohydrate has no strict floor and is the most flexible.

Protein factors shift with the goal: 1.6 to 2.2 g per kg while cutting to protect muscle in a deficit, 1.2 to 1.6 at maintenance, and 1.6 to 2.2 when building. Fat typically covers 20% to 35% of calories and should not sit below 20% for long, since hormones can suffer. Carbs absorb what is left and can vary with training, higher on training days and lower on rest days. Total energy drives weight change; the macro split shapes body composition, hunger and performance.
guide.tableTitle: Macro splits by goal (70 kg, TDEE 2,200 kcal)

faq.q: Can too much protein damage the kidneys?
faq.a: For healthy people, current evidence does not show harm from intakes up to about 2 grams per kilogram of bodyweight. Anyone diagnosed with chronic kidney disease does need to limit protein and should follow medical advice. Higher intakes also call for more water and enough fibre, so do not let meat crowd out vegetables and fruit.

faq.q: Do carbs or fat cause more weight gain?
faq.a: Neither is the culprit on its own; weight gain comes from a sustained calorie surplus. Fat is energy dense at 9 kcal per gram and easy to overeat unnoticed, while refined carbohydrate raises blood sugar quickly and satisfies poorly, so it is easy to overdo as well. In practice, controlling total calories while favouring filling foods such as protein, vegetables and whole grains works better than demonising one macro.

faq.q: Is a ketogenic diet suitable for most people?
faq.a: Keto, usually under 50 grams of carbohydrate a day, was developed to treat refractory epilepsy. Any fat loss advantage comes mainly from appetite suppression and easier calorie control rather than a metabolic edge. It is hard to sustain, often causes headache and fatigue at first, and long-term safety and adherence data are limited. Without a specific medical reason, most people do better with a moderate deficit and balanced nutrition.

faq.q: Do I need to hit the numbers exactly every day?
faq.a: No, and trying to is counterproductive. Macros average out over a day or a week, so a single day off changes nothing. Aim to hit your protein total across the week and let carbohydrate flex around training. Obsessing over grams tends to destroy adherence, and consistency over months matters far more than precision on any one day.

protein-calculator.name: Protein
protein-calculator.metaDescription: Calculate your daily protein needs based on your weight and goals

steps: Enter body weight (kg) and activity or fitness goal.
Pick goal: maintain / cut / bulk; protein scales accordingly.
See daily protein (g) and how many common-food servings that equals.
guide.explanationTitle: How much protein per day? Weight and goal
guide.formula: protein(g) ≈ weight(kg) × factor (maintain 0.8–1.2, bulk 1.6–2.2, cut 1.8–2.4)
explanation: Protein need is based on body weight, not total calories. Sedentary ~0.8 g/kg; regular lifters need 1.6–2.2 g/kg for synthesis and recovery.
During a cut, aim higher (1.8–2.4 g/kg): in a deficit, more protein preserves lean mass and boosts satiety. Older adults should also nudge it up.
The tool converts grams into servings of chicken, eggs, Greek yogurt, etc., turning an abstract number into a plate you can build.

faq.q: Does too much protein hurt kidneys?
faq.a: For normal kidney function, evidence doesn't support harm from high protein; those with chronic kidney disease should follow medical limits. For most, weight-based intake is safe.

faq.q: Is plant protein enough?
faq.a: Yes, but vary sources (legumes + grains) to cover essential amino acids. If fully vegan, aim slightly above the suggestion.

faq.q: How much per meal absorbs best?
faq.a: About 20–40 g quality protein per meal uses well; 3–4 meals beats one large dose for synthesis.

carb-calculator.name: Carbohydrate
carb-calculator.metaDescription: Calculate your optimal daily carbohydrate intake for energy and performance

steps: Enter your daily calorie target and your chosen carbohydrate percentage.
Add your activity level or goal if the tool uses it to suggest calories.
Read the grams of carbohydrates to aim for each day.
guide.formula: Carb grams = (Calories x carb%) / 4  (carbs = 4 kcal per gram)
explanation: Carbohydrates supply about 4 kilocalories per gram; setting a percentage turns your calorie goal into a gram target.
The right share depends on your goal, training, and preferences; many people do well across a wide range of carb intakes.

faq.q: How many carbs should I eat?
faq.a: It varies; a common range is 45 to 65 percent of calories, but athletes or low-carb dieters may differ.

faq.q: Are all carbs the same?
faq.a: No. Whole grains, fruit, and vegetables add fibre and nutrients, while added sugars give quick energy with little else.

faq.q: Why 4 calories per gram?
faq.a: That is the average energy yield of carbohydrate; protein is also 4, fat is 9 per gram.

fat-intake.name: Fat Intake
fat-intake.metaDescription: Calculate your daily fat intake needs including healthy fat sources

steps: Enter your daily calorie goal and a target fat percentage.
Choose whether to see grams of total fat or split into saturated and unsaturated.
Read the grams of fat that fit your plan.
guide.formula: Fat grams = (Calories x fat%) / 9  (fat = 9 kcal per gram)
explanation: Fat provides about 9 kilocalories per gram, more than twice carbs or protein, so small amounts contribute a lot of energy.
The type of fat matters: unsaturated fats from plants and fish are generally favorable, while excess saturated and trans fats are not.

faq.q: What fat percentage is healthy?
faq.a: Many guidelines suggest 20 to 35 percent of calories from fat, emphasising unsaturated sources.

faq.q: Why does fat have more calories?
faq.a: Its chemical structure stores more energy per gram, which is why 9 kcal per gram versus 4 for carbs and protein.

faq.q: Should I avoid all fat?
faq.a: No. Fat supports hormones, nerves, and vitamin absorption; choose quality sources and watch total amounts.

water-intake.name: Water Intake
water-intake.metaDescription: Calculate how much water you should drink daily based on your lifestyle

steps: Enter your body weight and choose kilograms or pounds.
Fill in how long and how hard you train, since sweat losses raise requirements substantially.
If you are in heat or at altitude, tick those options to account for the extra loss.
guide.explanationTitle: How daily water needs are estimated
guide.formula: Base need = weight (kg) × 30–35 ml; exercise = training minutes × extra factor
explanation: The most common rule is body weight times 30 to 35 millilitres, so a 60 kg person needs roughly 1.8 to 2.1 litres a day. That coefficient comes from measured daily losses through urine, breathing, skin evaporation and stool. For exercise, add roughly 350 to 700 ml per hour depending on intensity and how much you sweat.

One widespread misunderstanding deserves clearing up: the famous eight glasses, about two litres, is a memorable approximation that ignores weight, climate and activity. Just as importantly, that total does not all have to come from drinking, because food, especially fruit, vegetables and soups, supplies 20% to 30% of daily water, and metabolism generates around 300 ml. That means plain drinking water usually accounts for 500 to 800 ml less than the headline total. The simplest check is urine colour: pale straw means you are well hydrated, dark amber means drink more.
guide.tableTitle: Daily water suggestions by weight and activity

faq.q: Do coffee and tea count towards hydration?
faq.a: Yes. Caffeine has a mild diuretic effect, but at normal intakes the net effect is still hydrating, and research generally counts coffee and tea towards daily fluid intake. What deserves attention are sugary drinks and alcohol: the first add calories, and the second is clearly diuretic and increases fluid loss.

faq.q: If I feel thirsty, am I already dehydrated?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Thirst is a reliable signal for most healthy adults and typically kicks in at about 1% to 2% fluid loss, a level that does not harm performance or health. Thirst does blunt with age, however, and children often forget to drink when absorbed in play, so both groups benefit from drinking on a schedule rather than waiting.

faq.q: Is more water always better?
faq.a: No. The kidneys can excrete only about 800 to 1,000 ml per hour, so drinking very large volumes quickly can cause hyponatraemia, with headache, nausea and confusion, and in extreme cases it is life threatening. It is most often seen after endurance events when people replace sweat with plain water and no electrolytes. Drinking steadily to thirst is enough for everyday life.

faq.q: Do I need a sports drink when exercising?
faq.a: It depends on duration and intensity. Up to about 60 minutes of easy to moderate work, water suffices. Beyond 60 to 90 minutes, or when you sweat heavily, a drink with sodium, around 300 to 600 mg per litre, and 4% to 8% carbohydrate helps maintain electrolyte balance and glycogen. Weighing yourself before and after gives a practical target: replace roughly 1.2 to 1.5 litres for every kilogram lost.

body-type.name: Body Type
body-type.description: Determine your body type (ectomorph, mesomorph, endomorph)
body-type.metaDescription: Discover your body type and get personalized training and nutrition advice

steps: Answer a few questions about your build, or enter simple measurements.
Let the tool classify you into a somatotype or a blend.
Read the description and how it may relate to training and diet.
guide.formula: Descriptive classification, not a single formula
explanation: Somatotypes group builds into ectomorph (lean), mesomorph (muscular), and endomorph (rounder), though most people are a mix.
The model is a rough frame for training and nutrition, not a fixed destiny; genetics, diet, and exercise shape your actual results.

faq.q: Can my body type change?
faq.a: Yes. Training and diet shift your composition; the label is a starting point, not a life sentence.

faq.q: Which body type is best?
faq.a: None is superior; each has trade-offs, and mixed types are common and completely normal.

faq.q: Should I train only for my type?
faq.a: Use it as a guide, then follow evidence-based training and nutrition that fit your goals.

healthy-weight.name: Healthy Weight
healthy-weight.description: Calculate your healthy weight range based on height
healthy-weight.metaDescription: Find your healthy weight range based on your height, age, and frame size

steps: Enter your height, weight, age, and sex assigned at birth.
Choose the formula set if multiple are offered for your region.
Read your healthy weight range and where you currently fall within it.
guide.explanationTitle: Healthy weight ranges, not single numbers
guide.formula: Based on BMI 18.5 to 24.9 mapped back to weight = BMI x height^2
explanation: Healthy weight is shown as a range because a single number ignores body composition; muscle, bone, and frame size all shift what is right for you.
The range is a screening guide, not a diagnosis. Athletes and older adults especially should also consider body fat and waist circumference.

faq.q: Why a range and not one weight?
faq.a: People of the same height differ in muscle and bone, so a band captures normal variation better than a point.

faq.q: Is BMI enough?
faq.a: It is a useful screen but misses body composition; pair it with waist measurement and fitness.

faq.q: Does the range differ by ethnicity?
faq.a: Some guidelines use lower cut-offs for certain populations; check local public-health advice.

army-body-fat.name: Army Body Fat
army-body-fat.description: Calculate body fat using US Army standards
army-body-fat.metaDescription: Calculate your body fat percentage using the official US Army tape test method

steps: Enter the required measurements such as height, neck, and waist (and hips for some).
Choose the correct sex-specific formula.
Read your estimated body fat percentage and whether it meets the standard.
guide.formula: Uses circumference-based equations that differ for men and women
explanation: The method estimates body fat from tape measurements at the neck and waist, with hip circumference added for women, using sex-specific equations.
It is a field method: quick and repeatable, but less precise than DEXA or hydrostatic weighing, so treat results as estimates.

faq.q: Why measure the neck?
faq.a: The neck helps account for upper-body lean tissue, improving the estimate alongside waist size.

faq.q: Is it accurate?
faq.a: It is good for screening and tracking, but not a laboratory measurement; small tape errors change the result.

faq.q: Does it apply outside the military?
faq.a: The math works for anyone, but pass/fail standards are military-specific; consult your own guidelines.

bac-calculator.name: BAC
bac-calculator.metaDescription: Estimate your blood alcohol content based on drinks consumed

steps: Enter your sex, weight, number of standard drinks, and the hours spent drinking.
Add the drink strength and duration if a detailed mode is available.
Read your estimated blood alcohol concentration and the hours to sober up.
guide.formula: BAC = (A x 5.14 / W x r) - 0.015 x H  (A=oz alcohol, W=lb, r=0.73/0.66)
explanation: BAC estimates how much alcohol is in the bloodstream using the amount consumed, body water, and time for metabolism, which removes about 0.015 percent per hour.
It is only an estimate; food, medications, sleep, and tolerance change the real effect. Never use a number to decide if you can drive.

faq.q: What is a standard drink?
faq.a: Roughly 14 g of pure alcohol, about 350 ml beer, 150 ml wine, or 45 ml spirits, varying by strength.

faq.q: Can I drive at 0.02 percent?
faq.a: Laws differ and impairment begins with the first drink; if you have consumed alcohol, the safe choice is not to drive.

faq.q: Why does sex change the result?
faq.a: Average body water differs, so the same drinks produce a higher concentration for those with less water per kilogram.

gfr-calculator.name: GFR
gfr-calculator.description: Calculate glomerular filtration rate for kidney function
gfr-calculator.metaDescription: Calculate your eGFR to assess kidney function using CKD-EPI formula

steps: Enter your serum creatinine, age, and sex (and race coefficient if the older equation uses it).
Choose the equation, such as CKD-EPI or MDRD.
Read your estimated GFR and the corresponding kidney stage.
guide.formula: CKD-EPI and MDRD equations estimate GFR from creatinine, age, sex (and historically race)
explanation: eGFR estimates how well your kidneys filter waste; lower numbers mean reduced kidney function, grouped into stages 1 to 5.
It is a screening estimate from a blood test, not a diagnosis; only a clinician can interpret it alongside other tests.

faq.q: What is a normal eGFR?
faq.a: Around 90 or above is generally normal for adults, though it naturally declines a little with age.

faq.q: Why does race appear in some formulas?
faq.a: Older equations included a race coefficient, but current guidelines favour race-free versions to reduce bias.

faq.q: Should I worry about one low result?
faq.a: A single value can vary; your clinician looks at trends and other tests before drawing conclusions.

sleep-calculator.name: Sleep
sleep-calculator.description: Calculate optimal sleep and wake times
sleep-calculator.metaDescription: Find the best times to sleep and wake up based on sleep cycles

steps: Pick the time you plan to fall asleep, or the time you need to wake up.
Set how long you usually take to fall asleep, most people need 10 to 20 minutes, and the tool subtracts it.
Read the suggested times, all aligned to the end of complete sleep cycles.
guide.formula: Wake time = bedtime + time to fall asleep + cycles × 90 minutes (4–6 cycles)
explanation: Sleep unfolds in cycles of roughly 90 minutes, each containing light sleep (N1 and N2), deep sleep (N3) and rapid eye movement. Deep sleep dominates the first half of the night and handles physical repair and growth hormone release, while REM increases later and supports memory consolidation and emotional regulation. Waking at the end of a cycle, close to the surface, leaves you clear-headed, whereas being woken from deep sleep produces heavy sleep inertia and sluggishness.

So the calculator works from the moment you fall asleep, after subtracting the time it takes you to drift off, and steps forward in 90-minute blocks, listing the wake times for four, five and six cycles, which is 6, 7.5 and 9 hours. One caveat: 90 minutes is a population average, individual cycles run anywhere from 70 to 120 minutes and shorten slightly with age. Treat this as a practical scheduling aid rather than a precise read on your body clock.
guide.tableTitle: Cycle counts and total sleep

faq.q: Do I really need eight hours?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Eight is a round number that is easy to remember; real needs vary, and most adults fall somewhere between seven and nine hours. What matters more is completing whole cycles and how you feel on waking. If 7.5 hours leaves you sharp, there is no reason to force eight. The test is whether you feel sleepy during the day and struggle to get up.

faq.q: Why am I still tired after a long night?
faq.a: Often because you woke from deep sleep, or because quality was poor. Frequent awakenings, snoring with pauses in breathing, alcohol before bed, and a bedroom that is too bright or warm all reduce deep and REM sleep. If you consistently wake unrefreshed despite adequate hours, especially with loud snoring and morning headaches, ask about a sleep study.

faq.q: How long should a nap be?
faq.a: Ten to twenty minutes is ideal: it restores alertness without reaching deep sleep, so you wake clear-headed. Thirty to sixty minutes tends to end in deep sleep and produces noticeable grogginess. If you want a full cycle, allow 90 minutes. It also helps to nap before about 3 pm so night-time sleep is not affected.

faq.q: Does sleeping in at the weekend help?
faq.a: It repays part of the debt but cannot fully offset chronic short sleep, and it shifts your body clock, making Monday harder, the so-called social jetlag. Keeping bedtime and wake time within about an hour every day works better. If you are genuinely short, going to bed an hour earlier beats sleeping three hours later.

due-date.name: Due Date
due-date.description: Calculate pregnancy due date and milestones
due-date.metaDescription: Calculate your pregnancy due date and track important milestones

steps: Enter the first day of your last menstrual period (LMP).
The tool adds the standard 280 days (40 weeks) to estimate the due date.
See due date, current week, and key prenatal checkup milestones.
guide.explanationTitle: How due date is calculated: LMP and weeks
guide.formula: due = LMP + 280 days (Naegele: month+9, day+7)
explanation: The common method is Naegele's rule: from the first day of LMP, add 280 days (40 weeks). The shortcut is 'month+9, day+7'.
Only about 5% deliver exactly on the due date; within two weeks either side is normal. Early ultrasound (esp. CRL) refines the week better.
The tool also shows current gestational week and key screenings (NT, anatomy, glucose) so you can map the whole pregnancy timeline.

faq.q: Is the due date accurate?
faq.a: It's a midpoint estimate. ~80% are born within two weeks of it; only ~5% on the exact day. Treat it as a window, not a date.

faq.q: Irregular cycles?
faq.a: Long or irregular cycles make LMP-based dating early. First-trimester ultrasound (CRL) is more accurate.

faq.q: Why weeks, not months?
faq.a: Weeks (7-day) are finer; screenings are scheduled by week (NT 11–13, glucose 24–28), so weeks avoid missing windows.

ovulation-calculator.name: Ovulation
ovulation-calculator.description: Calculate ovulation date and fertile window
ovulation-calculator.metaDescription: Calculate your ovulation date and most fertile days

steps: Enter first day of last period and average cycle length (default 28).
The tool estimates ovulation (~14 days before next period) and the fertile window.
See estimated ovulation for the next 6 cycles to plan or avoid.
guide.explanationTitle: How to find ovulation: cycle and ovulation day
guide.formula: ovulation ≈ next period − 14 days; fertile ≈ 5 days before to 1 day after
explanation: Ovulation usually happens ~14 days before the next period (luteal phase is fairly fixed), while follicular length varies, so 'cycle−14' beats 'cycle÷2'.
Sperm survive ~3–5 days, egg ~12–24 h, so the fertile window spans ~5 days before to 1 day after ovulation—about a week.
Good for regular cycles as an estimate; for precision use basal temperature, OPKs, or an app. Irregular cycles widen the error.

faq.q: Can I calculate with irregular cycles?
faq.a: You can estimate but with larger error. The more variable the cycle, the harder ovulation is to predict—verify with OPK + temperature.

faq.q: Why is the fertile window so long?
faq.a: Sperm live for days and ovulation can shift, so covering the days around ovulation is safest.

faq.q: Used for both trying and avoiding?
faq.a: Yes, same principle: time intercourse for conception, or use protection to avoid—ovulation tracking alone isn't reliable birth control.

period-calculator.name: Period
period-calculator.description: Track menstrual cycle and predict next period
period-calculator.metaDescription: Track your menstrual cycle and predict your next period

steps: Enter first day of last period and average cycle length.
The tool estimates next period and upcoming cycle dates.
Also estimates the current phase (follicular / luteal).
guide.formula: next = last first day + cycle length; phase ≈ days since last first day
explanation: The core is cycle length: add one cycle to the last first day for the next expected date. Most people fall in 21–35 days; 28 is common, not a standard.
Knowing length also hints at phase: ovulation ~14 days before next period, follicular before, luteal after—helping explain mood/energy swings.
Good for regular-cycle reminders; if cycles are chaotic, very long, or painful, see a doctor for PCOS/thyroid rather than relying on math.

faq.q: What cycle length is normal?
faq.a: 21–35 days is common and varies by person. As long as yours is stable, you needn't hit 28.

faq.q: Why is mine never on time?
faq.a: Stress, big weight changes, poor sleep, illness all disrupt it. Occasional shifts are normal; chronic irregularity deserves a check.

faq.q: Can this detect pregnancy?
faq.a: No. A late period is only one possible sign; confirm with a test. This tool only schedules, not diagnoses.

pregnancy-weight-gain.name: Pregnancy Weight Gain
pregnancy-weight-gain.description: Calculate recommended weight gain during pregnancy
pregnancy-weight-gain.metaDescription: Calculate healthy weight gain recommendations during pregnancy

steps: Enter your pre-pregnancy weight and height to compute your starting BMI.
Select the recommended gain range for your BMI category.
Track your current gain against the suggested total for each trimester.
guide.formula: Total by BMI: underweight 12.5 to 18 kg, normal 11.5 to 16 kg, overweight 7 to 11.5 kg, obese 5 to 9 kg
explanation: Weight gain supports the baby, placenta, amniotic fluid, and maternal tissue stores; the right amount depends mainly on starting BMI.
Gaining too little or too much is linked to delivery and infant-health risks, so ranges are guidance, not strict rules, and your clinician individualizes them.

faq.q: What if I am expecting twins?
faq.a: Recommended totals are higher for multiples; follow your provider's specific schedule.

faq.q: Can I diet to lose weight while pregnant?
faq.a: Pregnancy is not the time for weight-loss dieting; focus on steady, adequate gain with good nutrition.

faq.q: Why does BMI at the start matter?
faq.a: It sets the safest gain band because risk patterns differ by starting weight.

basic-calculator.name: Basic
basic-calculator.description: Perform arithmetic calculations with expression support
basic-calculator.metaDescription: Free online basic calculator for arithmetic operations and expressions

steps: Type numbers using the on-screen pad or your keyboard.
Use + - x / and parentheses for the order of operations.
Read the result, and use clear or backspace to start a new calculation.
guide.formula: PEMDAS: Parentheses, Exponents, Multiplication/Division, Addition/Subtraction
explanation: The calculator follows standard precedence, so 2 + 3 x 4 equals 14, not 20; parentheses force a different grouping.
It is exact for the digits shown, but very long numbers are rounded for display; use scientific mode for high precision.

faq.q: Why is my answer different from expected?
faq.a: Check parentheses and operation order; multiplication runs before addition unless you group it.

faq.q: Does it keep history?
faq.a: This simple view shows the current line; use the expression history if your version includes it.

faq.q: Can it handle fractions?
faq.a: It works in decimals; convert fractions to decimals first for accurate results.

fraction-calculator.name: Fraction
fraction-calculator.description: Add, subtract, multiply, divide, and simplify fractions
fraction-calculator.metaDescription: Calculate fractions with step-by-step solutions and mixed numbers

steps: Pick an operation: add, subtract, multiply, divide, or just simplify a mixed/improper fraction.
Enter the numerators and denominators (multiple fractions supported); the tool validates that no denominator is zero.
Read the simplified result and toggle between improper and mixed-number display.
guide.formula: a/b ± c/d = (ad ± bc)/bd; (a/b) × (c/d) = ac/bd
explanation: A fraction has a numerator and a denominator: the denominator is how many equal parts the whole is split into, the numerator is how many of those parts you take. To add or subtract you must first rewrite both with a common denominator; multiply top-by-top and bottom-by-bottom; divide by multiplying by the reciprocal.

Results are usually reduced: divide numerator and denominator by their greatest common divisor to get the simplest form, and turn an improper fraction into a mixed number when the top is larger. Fraction arithmetic underpins ratios, probability, recipes and engineering measurement.

faq.q: Can the denominator be zero?
faq.a: No. Division by zero is undefined, so the calculator warns you the moment a denominator is zero to prevent invalid output.

faq.q: How do I enter a mixed number?
faq.a: Enter the whole part first, then the numerator and denominator; results can also be toggled between improper and mixed form for easier reading.

faq.q: Why is the result sometimes a repeating decimal?
faq.a: A fraction becomes a repeating decimal when its denominator has prime factors other than 2 or 5. That is normal, and you can keep as many digits as you need.

percentage-calculator.name: Percentage
percentage-calculator.description: Calculate percentages, percent change, and percent difference
percentage-calculator.metaDescription: Free online percentage calculator. Find X% of Y, what percent one number is of another, and increases or discounts fast, no signup.

steps: Pick the percentage operation you need (X% of Y, X is what % of Y, or increase/decrease).
Enter the numbers into the input fields.
Read the result instantly below the inputs.
guide.formula: Part = (Percentage / 100) × Whole
explanation: A percentage is simply a fraction of 100. Calculating 'X% of Y' means multiplying Y by X divided by 100.
Percentages are used daily for discounts, tax, tips, interest rates, and comparing changes between two values.

faq.q: How do I find what percent one number is of another?
faq.a: Divide the part by the whole and multiply by 100. For example, 25 of 200 is (25 / 200) × 100 = 12.5%.

faq.q: How do I calculate a percentage increase?
faq.a: Subtract the original from the new value, divide by the original, then multiply by 100.

faq.q: Can I use it for discounts?
faq.a: Yes. To find a sale price after a discount, calculate the percent of the original price and subtract it.

percent-error.name: Percent Error
percent-error.description: Calculate percent error between experimental and actual values
percent-error.metaDescription: Calculate percent error for scientific experiments and measurements

steps: Enter the measured (experimental) value and the accepted (true) value.
Choose whether to see the absolute error as well as the percentage.
Read the percent error, which tells you how far the measurement is from the reference.
guide.formula: Percent error = |measured - accepted| / |accepted| x 100%
explanation: Percent error expresses the size of a mistake relative to the true value, so a 5 percent error means the same proportion whether you measured grams or kilometres.
A smaller percent error means higher accuracy. Systematic errors from a faulty instrument show up as consistently biased results.

faq.q: Can percent error be negative?
faq.a: The formula uses absolute value, so it is reported as a positive magnitude; the sign is dropped to show size, not direction.

faq.q: What is a good percent error?
faq.a: It depends on the field; school labs often target under 5 percent, while precision engineering expects far less.

faq.q: Percent error vs percent difference?
faq.a: Error compares a measurement to a known true value; difference compares two measurements to each other.

rounding-calculator.name: Rounding
rounding-calculator.description: Round numbers using different methods and precision
rounding-calculator.metaDescription: Round numbers to decimal places, significant figures, or custom precision

steps: Enter the number you want to round and choose the target decimal places or significant figures.
Pick a rounding rule such as round half up or round to even if offered.
Read the rounded result and the digits that were kept.
guide.formula: Round to n decimals: keep n digits after the point, adjust the last kept digit by the next
explanation: Rounding reduces noise from measurements that are not exact, but repeated rounding can drift results, so round only at the final step.
Different rules (half up versus round to even) handle the exact .5 case differently, which matters in statistics and finance.

faq.q: What is round half to even?
faq.a: When the dropped part is exactly .5, round to the nearest even digit; this avoids bias when many .5 cases occur.

faq.q: Should I round during each step?
faq.a: No. Keep full precision while calculating and round only the final answer to avoid accumulating error.

faq.q: What are significant figures?
faq.a: They are the meaningful digits carried by a measurement's precision, counting from the first non-zero digit.

average-calculator.name: Average
average-calculator.description: Calculate mean, median, mode, and other averages
average-calculator.metaDescription: Calculate arithmetic mean, weighted average, geometric mean, and harmonic mean

steps: Enter the numbers line by line or comma separated; add or remove any time.
The tool ignores blank cells and flags obvious outliers (you can keep them if needed).
Read the arithmetic mean, the sum and the count, and toggle to see the median.
guide.formula: mean = (x₁ + x₂ + … + xₙ) ÷ n
explanation: The arithmetic mean adds up a set of values and divides by how many there are. It is a simple, intuitive measure of the 'centre' of the data, but it is very sensitive to extremes — a single very large or very small value can pull the mean noticeably up or down.

When a distribution is skewed or contains outliers, the median usually describes the typical value better than the mean. For example, a few very high incomes pull the average income up so most people appear 'below average'. Check both mean and median together.

faq.q: What is the difference between mean and median?
faq.a: The mean is the sum divided by the count; the median is the middle value after sorting. They diverge a lot in skewed data, and the median resists extreme values.

faq.q: Do empty cells affect the result?
faq.a: No. Blank cells and unrecognised text are ignored; only valid numbers are used.

faq.q: Can it do a weighted average?
faq.a: This tool computes the simple arithmetic mean. If each item has a different weight (e.g. exam weights), use a weighted average calculator.

long-division.name: Long Division
long-division.description: Perform long division with step-by-step solution
long-division.metaDescription: Learn long division with detailed step-by-step solutions and remainders

steps: Enter the dividend (the number being divided) and the divisor (the number you divide by).
Run the calculator to see the quotient and the remainder step by step.
Read the full decimal result and, if it does not divide evenly, the remainder.
guide.formula: dividend = divisor × quotient + remainder; 0 ≤ remainder < divisor
explanation: Long division repeatedly subtracts the largest multiple of the divisor that fits, bringing down digits until no remainder or a repeating decimal appears.
The remainder is what is left after the whole-number part of the quotient; it is always smaller than the divisor.

faq.q: What is the remainder?
faq.a: The leftover amount when the dividend is not a whole multiple of the divisor.

faq.q: Why does division sometimes repeat?
faq.a: Some fractions have denominators with prime factors other than 2 and 5, forcing a repeating decimal.

faq.q: Can the divisor be zero?
faq.a: No, division by zero is undefined and the calculator will reject it.

exponent-calculator.name: Exponent
exponent-calculator.metaDescription: Calculate powers, exponents, and exponential expressions

steps: Enter the base and the exponent you want to apply.
Choose whether the exponent is positive, negative, or fractional.
Read the result, noting that negative exponents mean division by the base.
guide.formula: a^n = a x a x ... (n times); a^-n = 1 / a^n; a^(1/n) = n-th root
explanation: An exponent tells you how many times to multiply the base by itself; a negative exponent flips it to a fraction, and a fractional one is a root.
Exponents turn repeated multiplication into a compact power, which is why they appear in growth, decay, and scientific notation.

faq.q: What does a negative exponent mean?
faq.a: It means one divided by the base raised to that power, so 2^-3 equals 1/8.

faq.q: How do I multiply powers?
faq.a: Keep the base and add exponents: a^m x a^n = a^(m+n).

faq.q: What is a fractional exponent?
faq.a: The denominator is the root; for example x^(1/2) is the square root of x.

root-calculator.name: Root
root-calculator.description: Calculate square roots, cube roots, and nth roots
root-calculator.metaDescription: Calculate square roots, cube roots, and any nth root of numbers

steps: Enter the radicand (the number under the root) and the index, such as 2 for square root.
Choose whether to allow complex results for negative inputs if offered.
Read the principal root and, for squares, the positive and negative values.
guide.formula: n-th root of x = y where y^n = x; square root means index 2
explanation: A root answers the question 'which number, raised to this power, gives the radicand'; the square root is the most common case.
Even roots of negative numbers are not real, so calculators either report an error or return a complex number depending on mode.

faq.q: Why are there two square roots?
faq.a: Both a positive and a negative number square to the same value; the principal root shown is the non-negative one.

faq.q: Can I take a root of a negative number?
faq.a: Odd roots (cube, etc.) of negatives are real, but even roots are not real unless complex mode is on.

faq.q: What is the index?
faq.a: It is the small number that says which root; 2 is square root, 3 is cube root, and so on.

logarithm-calculator.name: Logarithm
logarithm-calculator.metaDescription: Calculate logarithms with base 10, natural log, or any custom base

steps: Enter the number whose logarithm you need and pick the base, such as 10, e, or 2.
Choose natural log, common log, or a custom base if available.
Read the result, which is the exponent that reaches your number.
guide.formula: log_b(x) = y means b^y = x
explanation: A logarithm is the inverse of exponentiation: it tells you what power the base must be raised to in order to equal the number.
Logarithms compress huge ranges into manageable numbers, which is why they appear in pH, decibels, and earthquake magnitude.

faq.q: What is the difference between ln and log?
faq.a: ln uses base e (about 2.718); log usually means base 10 in many contexts, though some fields use log for base e.

faq.q: Can I take the log of zero or a negative?
faq.a: No real logarithm exists for zero or negatives; the result would require an impossible power.

faq.q: How do I change the base?
faq.a: Use the change-of-base rule: log_b(x) = log_k(x) / log_k(b) for any convenient base k.

quadratic-calculator.name: Quadratic Formula
quadratic-calculator.description: Solve quadratic equations and find roots
quadratic-calculator.metaDescription: Solve quadratic equations using the quadratic formula with step-by-step solutions

steps: Enter the coefficients a, b, and c from your quadratic equation a x^2 + b x + c = 0.
Make sure a is not zero, otherwise the equation is linear, not quadratic.
Read the roots, the discriminant, and whether the solutions are real or complex.
guide.formula: x = (-b ± √(b² - 4ac)) / (2a); discriminant D = b² - 4ac
explanation: The quadratic formula finds the two values of x where the parabola crosses the axis; the discriminant tells you how many real solutions exist.
If the discriminant is positive there are two real roots, zero gives one repeated root, and negative gives two complex conjugate roots.

faq.q: What does the discriminant tell me?
faq.a: Its sign reveals the nature of the roots: positive for two real, zero for one, negative for two complex.

faq.q: Why are there two answers?
faq.a: A squared term generally yields two symmetric solutions; the plus and minus in the formula captures both.

faq.q: What if a is zero?
faq.a: Then it is a linear equation with one solution; enter it into a linear solver instead.

factor-calculator.name: Factor
factor-calculator.description: Find all factors of a number
factor-calculator.metaDescription: Find all factors, factor pairs, and prime factors of any number

steps: Enter a positive integer you want to factor.
Run the calculator to list all factors or prime factors.
Read the factor pairs and, for prime factorization, the exponent form.
guide.formula: if n mod d = 0 then d is a factor; prime factors: n = p1^a1 × p2^a2 × ...
explanation: A factor divides a number with no remainder; the calculator tests divisors up to the square root to find them efficiently.
Prime factorization rewrites the number as a product of primes, which is the basis for GCD, LCM and simplifying fractions.

faq.q: What is the difference between factors and prime factors?
faq.a: Factors include composites like 6; prime factors are only the irreducible primes such as 2 and 3.

faq.q: Does 1 count as a factor?
faq.a: Yes, 1 and the number itself are always factors, but neither is prime.

faq.q: Why stop at the square root?
faq.a: Any factor larger than √n pairs with one smaller than √n, so testing beyond is redundant.

gcd-calculator.name: GCD
gcd-calculator.description: Calculate Greatest Common Divisor of multiple numbers
gcd-calculator.metaDescription: Calculate the greatest common divisor (GCD/GCF) of two or more numbers

steps: Enter two or more integers.
Run the calculator to find their greatest common divisor.
Read the GCD and, if needed, the steps using Euclid's algorithm.
guide.formula: gcd(a,b) = gcd(b, a mod b) until remainder is 0; last non-zero remainder is the gcd
explanation: The GCD is the largest integer that divides every input with no remainder; it is used to simplify fractions to lowest terms.
Euclid's algorithm replaces the larger number with the remainder repeatedly, which is far faster than testing every divisor.

faq.q: What is gcd used for?
faq.a: Simplifying fractions, and as a step in LCM and modular arithmetic.

faq.q: Is gcd of a negative number defined?
faq.a: Yes, gcd uses absolute values, so signs do not change the result.

faq.q: What if the numbers share no factor?
faq.a: Then the gcd is 1, and the numbers are called coprime.

lcm-calculator.name: LCM
lcm-calculator.description: Calculate Least Common Multiple of multiple numbers
lcm-calculator.metaDescription: Calculate the least common multiple (LCM) of two or more numbers

steps: Enter two or more integers.
Run the calculator to find their least common multiple.
Read the LCM, useful for adding fractions with different denominators.
guide.formula: lcm(a,b) = |a × b| / gcd(a,b); extend by pairing
explanation: The LCM is the smallest positive integer divisible by every input, handy when aligning cycles or adding unlike fractions.
It is computed via the GCD so it stays efficient even for large numbers, instead of listing multiples.

faq.q: When do I need LCM?
faq.a: Adding fractions with different denominators and finding common periods.

faq.q: What if one number is zero?
faq.a: LCM with zero is defined as zero, since zero is a multiple of every number.

faq.q: How is LCM linked to GCD?
faq.a: Their product equals the product of the numbers, so lcm = |a×b| / gcd.

prime-factorization.name: Prime Factorization
prime-factorization.description: Find prime factors and divisors of any number
prime-factorization.metaDescription: Find prime factorization, factor tree, and all divisors of any number

steps: Enter a positive integer greater than 1.
Run the calculator to break it into prime factors.
Read the prime list with exponents, e.g. 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5.
guide.formula: n = p1^a1 × p2^a2 × ... where each p is prime
explanation: Prime factorization expresses a number as a product of primes, the unique building blocks of every integer above 1.
It underpins GCD, LCM, cryptography and checking whether a number is prime or a perfect power.

faq.q: Why is it unique?
faq.a: The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic says every integer has exactly one prime factorization.

faq.q: What about 1?
faq.a: 1 is not prime and has no prime factors; factorization starts at 2.

faq.q: How large a number can it handle?
faq.a: Trial division is fine up to millions; huge numbers need advanced algorithms.

triangle-calculator.name: Triangle
triangle-calculator.description: Calculate triangle properties from sides and angles
triangle-calculator.metaDescription: Calculate triangle area, perimeter, angles, and sides with law of cosines

steps: Enter any three known values of a triangle, such as two sides and an angle.
Choose the solving method if several are possible for your inputs.
Read the missing sides, angles, area, and perimeter.
guide.formula: Law of sines: a/sin A = b/sin B; Law of cosines: c² = a² + b² - 2ab cos C
explanation: Given enough known parts, trigonometry finds the rest; which law to use depends on whether you know sides or angles.
The sum of interior angles is always 180 degrees, a key check that your solved triangle is valid.

faq.q: Which law should I use?
faq.a: Use the sine law when you have a side and its opposite angle; use the cosine law for two sides and the included angle.

faq.q: Why do my angles not add to 180?
faq.a: Rounding can cause small drift; keep full precision while solving and round only at the end.

faq.q: Can every set of inputs be solved?
faq.a: No. Some combinations, like three angles alone, leave the size undetermined.

pythagorean-calculator.name: Pythagorean Theorem
pythagorean-calculator.description: Calculate missing side using Pythagorean theorem
pythagorean-calculator.metaDescription: Find the missing side of a right triangle using the Pythagorean theorem

steps: State the known sides: legs a and b, or one leg and hypotenuse c.
Enter the known values and leave the unknown blank (you can solve for the hypotenuse only).
Read the third side and see the algebraic steps of the theorem.
guide.formula: a² + b² = c² (c is the hypotenuse)
explanation: The Pythagorean theorem says that in a right triangle, the square of the two legs equals the square of the hypotenuse. It is a foundation of Euclidean geometry and is used in construction, navigation, graphics and signal processing.
For the hypotenuse use √(a²+b²); if you know the hypotenuse and one leg, the other leg is √(c²−a²). It applies only to right triangles; others need the law of cosines.

faq.q: Only for right triangles?
faq.a: Yes. The theorem holds only for right triangles; general triangles use the law of cosines c²=a²+b²−2ab·cosC.

faq.q: How do I find the hypotenuse?
faq.a: Square the legs, add them, then take the square root: c = √(a²+b²).

faq.q: Must the units match?
faq.a: Yes. a, b and c must share one length unit, or the result is meaningless.

circle-calculator.name: Circle
circle-calculator.description: Calculate circle properties from radius, diameter, or circumference
circle-calculator.metaDescription: Calculate circle area, circumference, diameter, and radius

steps: Enter the radius, diameter, or circumference of the circle.
Let the tool derive the other measures from the one you provided.
Read the diameter, area, and circumference together.
guide.formula: C = 2πr, A = πr², d = 2r
explanation: A circle is fully described by its radius, so any one measure lets you compute the rest using pi.
Area grows with the square of the radius, which is why doubling the radius quadruples the area.

faq.q: What value of pi is used?
faq.a: Calculations use pi to many digits for accuracy; you only see it rounded in the display.

faq.q: How do I get area from diameter?
faq.a: First halve the diameter to get the radius, then apply A = πr².

faq.q: Why is circumference proportional to radius?
faq.a: The ratio of circumference to diameter is always pi, a constant for every circle.

area-calculator.name: Area
area-calculator.metaDescription: Calculate area of rectangle, square, circle, triangle, trapezoid, and more

steps: Pick a shape: rectangle, circle, triangle, trapezoid and more.
Enter the required dimensions (length/width, radius, base/height) as prompted.
Read the area and switch the unit freely (cm², m², inch², etc.).
guide.formula: rectangle = w×h; circle = πr²; triangle = base×height÷2
explanation: Area measures how much two-dimensional surface a shape covers, in square units. Each shape has its own formula: a rectangle is width times height, a circle is π times radius squared, a triangle is base times height divided by two.

Keep units consistent: if sides are in centimetres the result is in square centimetres, and mixing units produces wrong answers. Area comes up constantly in renovation, land, fabric cutting and packaging design.

faq.q: What if my units differ?
faq.a: Unify the side units first, or switch the result unit inside the tool, to avoid the 100× error from mixing cm and m.

faq.q: How do I find the area of an irregular shape?
faq.a: Split it into regular shapes, sum their areas, or use a grid estimate; for precision use a CAD tool.

faq.q: How many digits of π are used?
faq.a: The tool uses enough precision (about 3.14159) for daily use; specify more only in scientific work.

surface-area-calculator.name: Surface Area
surface-area-calculator.metaDescription: Calculate surface area of cube, sphere, cylinder, cone, and pyramid

steps: Select the 3D shape (box, sphere, cylinder, cone, etc.).
Enter its dimensions such as radius, height or side lengths.
Read the total surface area and, where useful, the lateral area separately.
guide.formula: box = 2(lw + lh + wh); sphere = 4πr²; cylinder = 2πr(r + h)
explanation: Surface area is the sum of the areas of all outer faces of a solid, measured in square units.
It matters for material needed to build, paint or wrap an object, unlike volume which measures capacity.

faq.q: Surface area vs volume?
faq.a: Area covers the outside (square units); volume fills the inside (cubic units).

faq.q: What is lateral area?
faq.a: The side surfaces only, excluding top and bottom bases.

faq.q: Why units squared?
faq.a: Area is two-dimensional, so the unit is raised to the second power.

volume-calculator.name: Volume
volume-calculator.metaDescription: Calculate volume of cube, sphere, cylinder, cone, prism, and more

steps: Pick a solid: cuboid, cube, cylinder, sphere, cone and more.
Enter the matching dimensions (length/width/height, radius, height).
Read the volume and switch units among mm³ / cm³ / m³ / L.
guide.formula: cuboid = l×w×h; cylinder = πr²h; sphere = 4/3·πr³
explanation: Volume is the space a three-dimensional object occupies, measured in cubic units. A cuboid is length × width × height; a cylinder is base area πr² times height; a sphere is 4/3πr³.
Watch the unit conversion: 1 cubic metre = 1000 litres. Liquids are usually given in litres or millilitres, solids in cm³. Volume matters for paint, packing boxes and aquarium capacity.

faq.q: Are volume and capacity the same?
faq.a: Close. Capacity is what a container holds (litres/mL); volume is the space an object takes (m³/cm³). The numbers convert directly.

faq.q: How do litres and cubic metres relate?
faq.a: 1 m³ = 1000 L, and 1 L = 1000 mL = 1000 cm³. The tool switches display for you.

faq.q: How do I measure an irregular object's volume?
faq.a: Use water displacement (submerge and read the rise in a graduated cylinder), or 3D scan and compute.

moment-of-inertia.name: Moment of Inertia Calculator
moment-of-inertia.description: Calculate second moment of area for various cross-sections
moment-of-inertia.metaDescription: Free moment of inertia calculator. Calculate second moment of area for rectangular, circular, I-beam, hollow, and custom cross-sections. Includes parallel axis theorem.

steps: Select the cross-section shape from the list or choose custom input.
Enter the required dimensions such as width, height, diameter, or radius.
Review the area moment of inertia and radius of gyration for bending and deflection calculations.
guide.explanationTitle: Area moment of inertia in beams
guide.formula: Rectangle: I = b × h^3 / 12; Circle: I = π × d^4 / 64
explanation: The area moment of inertia measures how a cross-section resists bending; larger values mean less deflection under the same load.
It depends on the shape and orientation of the cross-section, not on the material itself.
The radius of gyration relates the moment of inertia to the cross-sectional area and is useful for buckling analysis.

faq.q: Is this the same as mass moment of inertia?
faq.a: No; area moment of inertia relates to bending stiffness, while mass moment of inertia relates to rotational inertia.

faq.q: Why does orientation matter for a rectangle?
faq.a: A beam laid flat has a much lower I about the bending axis than the same beam standing upright.

faq.q: Can I use this for composite shapes?
faq.a: Yes, by splitting the section into simple shapes and applying the parallel axis theorem.

beam-deflection.name: Beam Deflection Calculator
beam-deflection.description: Calculate beam deflection, shear, and bending moment with diagrams
beam-deflection.metaDescription: Free beam deflection calculator. Analyze simply supported, cantilever, and fixed-fixed beams with point or distributed loads. Includes shear and moment diagrams.

steps: Select the beam support condition: cantilever, simply supported, or fixed ends.
Enter beam length, load magnitude, load position, and material properties like Young's modulus and moment of inertia.
Review the maximum deflection, reaction forces, and bending moment diagram summary.
guide.formula: Max deflection depends on load case; common case: δ_max = P × L^3 / (48 × E × I) for center point load
explanation: Beam deflection describes how much a structural member bends under applied loads without permanent deformation.
The deflection depends on load type, support conditions, span length, material stiffness, and cross-section shape.
Staying within allowable deflection limits prevents cracks in finishes and ensures serviceability.

faq.q: What is allowable deflection?
faq.a: Typical limits range from L/180 to L/360 of the span, depending on the building code and use.

faq.q: Does this calculator replace structural engineering review?
faq.a: No; it is an educational tool. Real designs require code checks for strength, stability, and safety factors.

faq.q: Can I combine multiple loads?
faq.a: Yes by superposition: calculate deflection for each load case and add the results if the system remains elastic.

stress-strain.name: Stress-Strain Calculator
stress-strain.description: Calculate stress, strain, and Young's modulus with material database
stress-strain.metaDescription: Free stress-strain calculator. Calculate engineering stress, strain, Young's modulus, and safety factor. Includes material database with 30+ materials (steel, aluminum, wood, concrete).

steps: Enter the applied force and the original cross-sectional area to compute stress.
Enter the change in length and original length to compute strain.
Review stress, strain, and Young's modulus if both stress and strain are provided.
guide.formula: Stress = force / area; Strain = change_in_length / original_length; E = stress / strain
explanation: Stress is the internal force distributed over a cross-section, measured in pascals or psi.
Strain is the deformation per unit length; it is dimensionless because it is a ratio of lengths.
Young's modulus is the slope of the elastic region and describes how stiff a material is under tension or compression.

faq.q: What units should I use?
faq.a: Use consistent units: newtons with square meters give pascals; pounds with square inches give psi.

faq.q: Can strain be greater than 1?
faq.a: Yes, but most engineering materials are designed to stay well below 1 in the elastic range.

faq.q: Is Young's modulus the same in tension and compression?
faq.a: For many materials it is approximately the same, but brittle materials can behave differently in compression.

column-buckling.name: Column Buckling Calculator
column-buckling.description: Calculate Euler critical load, AISC allowable load, and slenderness ratio for columns
column-buckling.metaDescription: Free column buckling calculator. Compute Euler critical load, AISC allowable stress, slenderness ratio, and effective length with material and section databases.

steps: Enter the column length, end fixity factor, cross-sectional area, and least moment of inertia.
Provide the material's modulus of elasticity and any applied axial load.
Review the critical buckling load and slenderness ratio to judge stability.
guide.formula: P_cr = π^2 × E × I / (K × L)^2
explanation: Euler buckling occurs when a slender column under compression suddenly deflects sideways.
The effective length factor K depends on how the ends are restrained; pinned ends use K=1.0, fixed ends use K=0.5.
The slenderness ratio tells you whether Euler theory applies; very short columns fail by crushing rather than buckling.

faq.q: What is the slenderness ratio limit for Euler buckling?
faq.a: Euler is generally valid when the slenderness ratio is above about 100 for steel, but codes provide specific transition limits.

faq.q: Does material strength affect Euler buckling?
faq.a: Not directly; Euler critical load depends only on elastic modulus, geometry, and length. Yield strength matters for inelastic buckling.

faq.q: Can I account for self-weight?
faq.a: This calculator uses an axial load you provide; add the column's self-weight to the applied load if it is significant.

pipe-flow.name: Pipe Flow Calculator
pipe-flow.description: Calculate pressure drop, Reynolds number, and friction factor for pipe flow
pipe-flow.metaDescription: Free pipe flow calculator. Compute Darcy-Weisbach pressure drop, Reynolds number, Colebrook-White friction factor, and head loss with pipe material and fluid databases.

steps: Enter the pipe inner diameter, pipe length, and roughness for the material.
Provide the fluid properties: density and dynamic viscosity, plus either flow rate or pressure drop.
Review the Reynolds number, friction factor, head loss, and velocity.
guide.formula: Head loss = f × (L/D) × (v^2 / (2g)); Reynolds number = ρ × v × D / μ
explanation: The Reynolds number tells you whether the flow is laminar, transitional, or turbulent.
The Darcy friction factor depends on Reynolds number and pipe roughness; it links velocity to pressure drop.
Head loss is the energy lost per unit weight of fluid due to friction along the pipe.

faq.q: What is the difference between Darcy and Fanning friction factor?
faq.a: Darcy-Weisbach uses the Darcy friction factor, which is four times the Fanning friction factor.

faq.q: Can I use this for gases?
faq.a: Yes for incompressible approximations; for long pipelines or high pressure drops, compressible flow corrections are needed.

faq.q: Does the calculator include minor losses from fittings?
faq.a: No; it computes major frictional losses only. Add fitting losses separately using loss coefficients.

engineering-unit-converter.name: Engineering Unit Converter
engineering-unit-converter.description: Convert between engineering units: force, pressure, stress, torque, and more
engineering-unit-converter.metaDescription: Free engineering unit converter with NIST-precision factors. Convert force, pressure, stress, torque, density, length, area, moment of inertia, and section modulus.

steps: Select the physical quantity you want to convert, such as force, pressure, stress, torque, density, or energy.
Enter the value and choose the source unit and target unit.
Review the converted value and the conversion factor used.
guide.formula: Result = input_value × (target_unit_in_base / source_unit_in_base)
explanation: Engineering calculations fail when units are mixed; converting everything to a consistent system avoids order-of-magnitude errors.
The SI system uses newtons, pascals, and meters, while the US customary system uses pounds, psi, and inches.
Some units like mass density and specific weight look similar but have different dimensions and must not be interchanged.

faq.q: What is the difference between mass and force units?
faq.a: Mass is measured in kilograms or slugs; force is measured in newtons or pounds. On Earth, weight is a force equal to mass times gravity.

faq.q: Can I convert between SI and US units?
faq.a: Yes; the calculator handles common conversions between metric and US customary engineering units.

faq.q: Why does pressure use both Pa and N/m^2?
faq.a: Pascal and newton per square meter are the same unit; different names are used in different engineering fields.

molecular-weight.name: Molecular Weight Calculator
molecular-weight.description: Calculate molar mass and composition from chemical formula
molecular-weight.metaDescription: Free molecular weight calculator. Calculate molar mass, element composition, and mass percentage from chemical formulas (H2O, Ca(OH)2, CuSO4·5H2O). Includes 118 elements from IUPAC 2024.

steps: Enter a chemical formula such as H2O or C6H12O6.
Let the tool sum the atomic masses of each element.
Read the molar mass in grams per mole.
guide.formula: Molar mass = sum of (atoms of element x atomic mass)
explanation: Molecular weight is the sum of the atomic masses of all atoms in a formula, using standard atomic weights from the periodic table.
It bridges the microscopic (atoms) and macroscopic (grams) worlds, letting you weigh out a known number of moles.

faq.q: What is the difference between mass and weight here?
faq.a: In practice the terms are used interchangeably for this value, though strictly mass is the physical quantity.

faq.q: Why does water equal 18?
faq.a: H is about 1 and O about 16, so H2O is 2x1 + 16 = 18 grams per mole.

faq.q: Does it work for hydrates?
faq.a: Yes, include the water of crystallisation in the formula, for example CuSO4·5H2O.

molarity.name: Molarity Calculator
molarity.description: Calculate solution concentration from mass, moles, and volume
molarity.metaDescription: Free molarity calculator. Calculate solution concentration (M, mM, µM, nM) from mass/volume or moles/volume with step-by-step calculations.

steps: Enter the moles of solute and the volume of solution in litres.
Adjust units if the tool lets you switch between molar, millimolar, and so on.
Read the concentration in moles per litre, or M.
guide.formula: M = moles of solute / litres of solution
explanation: Molarity counts how many moles of a substance are dissolved in one litre of solution, the most common lab concentration unit.
Because it is per litre of final solution (not solvent), dilution changes molarity while the amount of solute stays the same.

faq.q: Moles vs molar, what is the difference?
faq.a: A mole is an amount of substance; molar (M) is that amount per litre of solution.

faq.q: How do I make a solution of a target M?
faq.a: Dissolve the needed moles (mass divided by molar mass) and then add solvent up to the final volume.

faq.q: Why does temperature matter?
faq.a: Volume changes slightly with temperature, so molarity is technically temperature dependent; molality is not.

dilution.name: Dilution Calculator
dilution.description: Calculate dilution parameters using M₁V₁ = M₂V₂ formula
dilution.metaDescription: Free dilution calculator. Calculate initial volume, final volume, or final molarity using M₁V₁ = M₂V₂ with serial dilution support and safety warnings.

steps: Enter the starting concentration and volume, and either the target concentration or target volume.
Let the tool compute the missing value using the dilution relationship.
Read how much solvent to add or what final volume to reach.
guide.formula: C1 x V1 = C2 x V2
explanation: Dilution keeps the amount of solute constant while adding solvent, so the product of concentration and volume stays equal before and after.
It is the backbone of preparing standards and dosing liquids; always add solvent to reach the final volume, not just mix equal parts.

faq.q: What does C1V1 = C2V2 mean?
faq.a: The moles of solute before equal the moles after; concentration drops as volume rises.

faq.q: Do units need to match?
faq.a: Concentration units must match on both sides, and volume units must match; the ratio is what matters.

faq.q: Can I dilute to any concentration?
faq.a: Yes mathematically, but practical limits include measurement precision and solubility.

stoichiometry.name: Stoichiometry Calculator
stoichiometry.description: Calculate limiting reactant and theoretical yield from chemical equations
stoichiometry.metaDescription: Free stoichiometry calculator. Calculate limiting reactant, theoretical yield, and product masses from balanced chemical equations. Shows mole ratios and step-by-step calculations.

steps: Enter a balanced chemical equation and the amount of one reactant or product.
Let the tool use mole ratios from the coefficients to find the others.
Read the moles or mass of the substance you asked about.
guide.formula: Amount B = Amount A x (coefficient B / coefficient A)
explanation: Stoichiometry uses the coefficients of a balanced equation as mole ratios to predict how much product forms or reactant is needed.
It assumes the reaction goes to completion with no side reactions, which real experiments only approximate.

faq.q: Why must the equation be balanced?
faq.a: Conservation of mass requires equal atoms on both sides, and the coefficients give the mole ratios.

faq.q: What is the limiting reactant?
faq.a: The reactant that runs out first, which caps how much product can form.

faq.q: Does this predict actual yield?
faq.a: It gives the theoretical yield; real yield is lower due to losses and incomplete reaction.

ph-calculator.name: pH Calculator
ph-calculator.description: Calculate pH, pOH, and ion concentrations for acids, bases, and buffers
ph-calculator.metaDescription: Free pH calculator. Calculate pH/pOH from concentration, strong/weak acids/bases, and buffer solutions using Henderson-Hasselbalch equation. Includes pH scale visualization.

steps: Enter the hydrogen ion concentration, or the acid and its concentration.
Choose whether to compute pH, pOH, or convert between them.
Read the pH and what it implies about acidity or basicity.
guide.formula: pH = -log10[H+]; pOH = 14 - pH (at 25 C)
explanation: pH is the negative base-10 logarithm of hydrogen ion concentration, so each unit is a tenfold change in acidity.
A pH below 7 is acidic, 7 neutral, above 7 basic; the scale is temperature dependent and the 0 to 14 range is typical for water-based solutions.

faq.q: Why is pH logarithmic?
faq.a: Because ion concentrations span many orders of magnitude, a log scale keeps them on a handy 0 to 14 range.

faq.q: Is 7 always neutral?
faq.a: Neutral is where pH equals pOH; at 25 C that is 7, but the neutral point shifts with temperature.

faq.q: Can pH be negative?
faq.a: Yes, very concentrated strong acids can have pH below 0, though that is unusual in everyday contexts.

periodic-table.name: Periodic Table
periodic-table.description: Interactive periodic table with element properties and search
periodic-table.metaDescription: Interactive periodic table with 118 elements. Search by name, symbol, or atomic number. View atomic mass, electron configuration, and chemical properties from IUPAC 2024 data.

steps: Enter an element symbol or atomic number to look it up.
Browse or filter by group, period, or category if offered.
Read properties such as atomic mass, group, and classification.
guide.explanationTitle: The periodic table at a glance
guide.formula: Organised by increasing atomic number and electron shells
explanation: The table arranges elements by atomic number; rows are periods and columns are groups with similar chemistry.
Position predicts behaviour: metals, nonmetals, and noble gases cluster in regions, making trends like electronegativity easy to read.

faq.q: What does the atomic number mean?
faq.a: It is the count of protons in the nucleus and uniquely identifies each element.

faq.q: Why are some elements grouped?
faq.a: Elements in the same column share valence-electron patterns, so they react in similar ways.

faq.q: What are the blocks?
faq.a: s, p, d, and f blocks reflect which subshell is being filled, linking position to electron structure.

vm-storage-calculator.name: VM Storage Calculator
vm-storage-calculator.description: Calculate vSphere ESX cluster storage capacity requirements
vm-storage-calculator.metaDescription: Free VMware vSphere storage calculator. Calculate VM storage capacity including provisioned disk, swap files, snapshots, and growth allocation. Supports thick and thin provisioning.

steps: Enter the number of VMs, average disk size per VM, and the RAID/erasure overhead factor.
Enter growth rate and snapshot retention you plan to keep.
Read the total raw and usable capacity required before provisioning storage.
guide.formula: usable = VMs × diskGB × (1 + overhead); raw = usable / raidEfficiency
explanation: Virtual environments need overhead for snapshots, replicas and RAID parity, so usable capacity is always less than raw disks.
Plan for at least 20–30% free headroom so live migration and patching never stall when a datastore fills up.

faq.q: Why is usable less than raw?
faq.a: RAID parity, erasure coding and snapshots consume capacity before any guest data is stored.

faq.q: How much headroom should I keep?
faq.a: Aim for 20–30% free to absorb spikes, snapshots and maintenance operations.

faq.q: Do thin provisioned disks save space?
faq.a: They delay usage but the total logical size still must fit the datastore when fully written.

k8s-capacity-calculator.name: Kubernetes Capacity Calculator
k8s-capacity-calculator.description: Calculate Kubernetes cluster node requirements for your workload
k8s-capacity-calculator.metaDescription: Free Kubernetes capacity planning calculator. Calculate nodes needed for K8s cluster based on pod CPU/memory requests, system reserved resources, and target utilization. Shows limiting factor (CPU vs memory).

steps: Enter the CPU and memory requests of a single pod and how many replicas you run.
Enter node size (CPU/memory) and the system reservation overhead.
Read how many nodes are needed and the cluster utilization before deploying.
guide.formula: nodes = ceil(totalReq / (nodeCap × (1 - sysReserve))); util = totalReq / (nodes × nodeCap)
explanation: Kubernetes schedules on requests, not limits, so you must size for the sum of requests plus a buffer for system pods and bin-packing inefficiency.
Reserving 10–20% of each node for kube-system and eviction thresholds prevents the scheduler from marking nodes unschedulable under load.

faq.q: Requests or limits drive scheduling?
faq.a: Scheduling uses requests; limits only cap usage and can cause OOM if set too low.

faq.q: Why reserve node capacity?
faq.a: kube-system pods and eviction thresholds need headroom or nodes become unschedulable.

faq.q: How do I improve bin-packing?
faq.a: Right-size requests, use topology spread and avoid tiny nodes that waste reservation overhead.

server-virtualization-calculator.name: Server Virtualization Calculator
server-virtualization-calculator.description: Calculate ESX host requirements for VM workloads
server-virtualization-calculator.metaDescription: Free VMware ESX host sizing calculator. Calculate required hosts based on VM CPU/RAM requirements with N+1 high availability support.

steps: Enter the number of physical servers and their average CPU/RAM utilization today.
Enter target consolidation ratio and the specs of the new virtual host.
Read the reduced host count, power savings and rack space freed.
guide.formula: hostsNeeded = ceil(physicalLoad / (hostCap × consolRatio)); savedPower = physicalPower - hostsNeeded × hostPower
explanation: Virtualization lets many underused physical servers share fewer, larger hosts, raising utilization from often under 15% to 60–80%.
The biggest wins are fewer units to power and cool, less rack space, and simpler hardware lifecycle management.

faq.q: What consolidation ratio is realistic?
faq.a: Ratios of 10:1 to 20:1 are common for general workloads, less for latency-sensitive ones.

faq.q: Does virtualization always cut power?
faq.a: Yes on total facility power, though each host draws more than the old servers it replaces.

faq.q: What about licensing?
faq.a: Hypervisor and guest OS licenses can offset savings, so model them before committing.

vmware-licensing-calculator.name: VMware Licensing Calculator
vmware-licensing-calculator.metaDescription: Free VMware licensing cost calculator. Calculate VMware Cloud Foundation and vSphere Foundation subscription costs with 16-core minimum enforcement.

steps: Enter the number of CPU cores or processors across your hosts that need licensing.
Select the VMware edition and any add-on packs you require.
Read the total license key count and estimated subscription cost before purchase.
guide.formula: licenses = sum(hostProcessors × coresPerProc, capped per key); cost = licenses × editionPrice
explanation: VMware is typically licensed per physical processor (socket) with a minimum core count per socket, so counting cores correctly avoids costly shortfalls.
Edition and support tier drive price far more than raw core count, so compare Standard vs Enterprise plus required add-ons like vSAN or NSX.

faq.q: Is VMware licensed per core or per socket?
faq.a: Per CPU socket, with a minimum number of cores per socket that must be licensed even if unused.

faq.q: Do I license vCenter separately?
faq.a: Yes, vCenter Server is licensed per instance on top of the ESXi host licenses.

faq.q: What about stagnant SNL contracts?
faq.a: Support and subscription (SnS) renewals often dominate lifetime cost, so model them over 3–5 years.

virtualization-cost.name: Virtualization Cost Calculator
virtualization-cost.description: Calculate total cost of ownership for virtualization infrastructure
virtualization-cost.metaDescription: Free virtualization TCO calculator. Calculate total cost of ownership including CAPEX and OPEX for virtualization infrastructure.

steps: Enter the number of hosts, their purchase price and expected lifespan.
Enter power, cooling, licensing and admin hours per year.
Read the total cost of ownership and cost per VM over the period.
guide.formula: tco = capEx + years × (power + cooling + licenses + labor); costPerVM = tco / totalVMs
explanation: Virtualization TCO includes one-time hardware plus recurring power, cooling, software licenses and staff time, and ignoring any one distorts the comparison.
Dividing TCO by the number of VMs you run shows whether consolidating onto fewer, denser hosts actually lowers cost per workload.

faq.q: What is the biggest hidden cost?
faq.a: Software licensing and admin labor usually exceed the hardware itself over a 3–5 year span.

faq.q: Should I include power and cooling?
faq.a: Yes, in a data center they can equal or exceed hardware depreciation annually.

faq.q: Does more VMs always lower cost per VM?
faq.a: Only up to the point where density hurts performance or reliability; then outages cost more than hardware.

hyperv-consolidation.name: Hyper-V Consolidation Calculator
hyperv-consolidation.description: Calculate Hyper-V host requirements with HA and Windows licensing
hyperv-consolidation.metaDescription: Free Hyper-V consolidation calculator. Calculate required hosts with N+1/N+2 HA, storage stacking, and Windows Server licensing costs.

steps: Enter your current count of physical servers and their average CPU/RAM usage.
Enter the target Hyper-V host size and desired reserve headroom.
Read the projected host count, consolidation ratio and freed rack units.
guide.formula: hosts = ceil(totalLoad / (hostCap × (1 - reserve))); ratio = physicalServers / hosts
explanation: Hyper-V lets you collapse many lightly used physical boxes onto a few hosts running Windows Server with the Hyper-V role.
Keeping 15–25% headroom per host preserves live-migration capacity so maintenance or a host failure never disrupts running VMs.

faq.q: What reserve should each host keep?
faq.a: Plan 15–25% free so failover clusters can absorb a downed node without overcommit.

faq.q: Core licensing implications?
faq.a: Windows Server is licensed per core, so larger hosts raise OS license cost even as VM count drops.

faq.q: Is failover clustering required?
faq.a: Not required, but it is what makes consolidation safe by allowing automatic VM restart.

windows-licensing.name: Windows Server Licensing Calculator
windows-licensing.description: Compare Datacenter vs Standard licensing costs
windows-licensing.metaDescription: Free Windows Server licensing calculator. Compare Datacenter and Standard editions with break-even analysis and 16-core minimum enforcement.
