steps: Enter the number of physical cores in each Windows Server host.
Select the edition and the licensing model (per core with CALs, or subscription).
Read the minimum core licenses required and total cost including CALs.
guide.formula: coreLicenses = max(16, coresPerHost) × hosts; cost = coreLicenses × corePrice + cals × calPrice
explanation: Windows Server is licensed per physical core with a minimum of 16 cores per server, so small servers still buy a 16-core pack.
User/Device CALs are licensed separately and are easy to forget; the model you pick changes the breakeven dramatically at scale.

faq.q: What is the minimum cores per server?
faq.a: 16 cores; even a 4-core box requires 16 core licenses.

faq.q: Are CALs always required?
faq.a: For most on-prem access models yes, though Azure Stack HCI and subscription options differ.

faq.q: Standard vs Datacenter?
faq.a: Standard covers limited OSEs per host; Datacenter is better when you run many VMs per host.

hypervisor-comparison.name: Hypervisor Comparison Calculator
hypervisor-comparison.description: Compare VMware, Hyper-V, Proxmox, and XCP-ng platforms
hypervisor-comparison.metaDescription: Free hypervisor comparison calculator. Compare VMware vSphere, Microsoft Hyper-V, Proxmox VE, and XCP-ng with TCO analysis, sizing, and feature matrix.
hypervisor-comparison.windowsEditionHint: Standard is cheaper for <13 VMs/host, Datacenter for more.

steps: Enter your workload profile: VM count, OS mix, and whether you need live migration.
Select candidate hypervisors and their licensing or support costs.
Read the feature and cost comparison to pick the best fit.
guide.formula: score = w1×features + w2×(1/cost) + w3×support; pick max(score)
explanation: Hypervisors differ in licensing model (free, per-core, subscription), ecosystem maturity and management tooling, not just raw performance.
The cheapest option can become the most expensive if it lacks the automation, backup or support your team depends on daily.

faq.q: Is free hypervisor good enough?
faq.a: For labs yes, but production usually needs support, live migration and backup APIs that free tiers omit.

faq.q: What matters most for selection?
faq.a: Match feature depth to your actual ops: backups, HA, and management tooling often beat raw speed.

faq.q: Should I consider lock-in?
faq.a: Yes, VM format and management portability affect future migration cost between platforms.

slope-calculator.name: Slope
slope-calculator.description: Calculate slope, equation, and angle of a line
slope-calculator.metaDescription: Calculate slope, y-intercept, and linear equation from two points

steps: Enter the coordinates of two points, (x1, y1) and (x2, y2).
Run the calculator to compute the slope and y-intercept.
Read the slope m, intercept b and the line equation y = mx + b.
guide.explanationTitle: Finding the slope of a line
explanation: Slope measures how steep a line is: rise over run, or the change in y per unit change in x.
A positive slope rises left to right, negative falls, zero is flat, and an undefined slope is a vertical line.

faq.q: What if x values are equal?
faq.a: The line is vertical and slope is undefined (division by zero).

faq.q: What does a slope of 1 mean?
faq.a: The line rises one unit vertically for every one unit horizontally, a 45° angle.

faq.q: How do I get the equation?
faq.a: Once m is known, b = y − mx at either point gives y = mx + b.

standard-deviation.name: Standard Deviation
standard-deviation.metaDescription: Free online standard deviation calculator. Find population or sample SD and variance fast, no signup, with clear formula and examples.

steps: Enter your data set as a list of numbers separated by commas.
Choose whether it is a population or a sample.
Read the result: the calculator shows the standard deviation and the variance.
guide.formula: σ = √( Σ(xᵢ − μ)² / N )   (population)
explanation: Standard deviation measures how spread out the values in a data set are around the mean. A small value means the numbers are clustered closely together, while a large value means they vary widely.
Use it to compare consistency between groups, assess risk in finance, or understand variation in test scores and scientific measurements.

faq.q: Population or sample — which should I pick?
faq.a: Use population when you have every member of the group (e.g. all students in a class). Use sample when your data is only a subset and you want to estimate the whole population.

faq.q: Why is the sample standard deviation larger?
faq.a: The sample formula divides by n−1 instead of n, which corrects the bias from estimating the mean from the same data, giving a slightly larger, more honest spread.

faq.q: What unit is the result in?
faq.a: The standard deviation always uses the same unit as your original data, which makes it easy to interpret alongside the mean.

statistics-calculator.name: Statistics
statistics-calculator.description: Calculate comprehensive statistics for a data set
statistics-calculator.metaDescription: Free online statistics calculator. Get mean, median, mode, range and standard deviation from a list fast, no signup, with clear explanation.

steps: Enter your numbers as a comma-separated list.
The calculator computes mean, median, mode, range, and standard deviation.
Use the summary to understand the shape and spread of your data.
guide.formula: Mean = Σx / n
explanation: Descriptive statistics summarize a data set with a few meaningful numbers. The mean shows the center, while the range and standard deviation show the spread.
These measures help you compare groups, spot outliers, and communicate findings clearly without plotting every point.

faq.q: What is the difference between mean and median?
faq.a: The mean is the average of all values; the median is the middle value when sorted. The median is less affected by extreme outliers.

faq.q: When should I use the mode?
faq.a: Use the mode when you want the most frequently occurring value, common in categories and discrete counts.

faq.q: Why does spread matter?
faq.a: Two data sets can share the same mean but behave very differently; spread measures reveal that difference.

probability-calculator.name: Probability
probability-calculator.description: Calculate probability of events and combinations
probability-calculator.metaDescription: Free online probability calculator. Find the chance of single or combined events fast, no signup, shown as fraction, decimal and percent.

steps: Choose the probability scenario (single event, two events, or combinations).
Enter the numbers of favorable and total outcomes.
Read the probability as a fraction, decimal, and percentage.
guide.formula: P = Favorable outcomes / Total outcomes
explanation: Probability quantifies how likely an event is, from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). It is the ratio of favorable outcomes to all possible outcomes.
It underpins games of chance, risk assessment, quality control, and any decision made under uncertainty.

faq.q: What does a probability of 0.5 mean?
faq.a: It means the event is as likely to happen as not — a 50% chance, like a fair coin landing heads.

faq.q: How is probability written?
faq.a: As a fraction, a decimal between 0 and 1, or a percentage between 0% and 100%.

faq.q: Can probabilities be added?
faq.a: Only for mutually exclusive events. Otherwise you must account for overlap to avoid double-counting.

sample-size.name: Sample Size
sample-size.description: Calculate required sample size for surveys and studies
sample-size.metaDescription: Free online sample size calculator. Find how many responses you need for a given confidence and margin of error, no signup, with steps.

steps: Enter your confidence level, margin of error, and an estimate of the population proportion.
Add the population size if it is small and known.
Read the required sample size to reach a reliable conclusion.
guide.formula: n = z² · p(1−p) / e²   (with finite-population correction)
explanation: Sample size is how many observations you need to estimate a population value within a given margin of error at a chosen confidence level.
Too small a sample gives unreliable results; too large wastes effort. The calculator balances precision against cost.

faq.q: What confidence level should I use?
faq.a: 95% is the most common default in research; 99% gives more certainty but requires a larger sample.

faq.q: What if I don't know the population proportion?
faq.a: Use 0.5 (50%), which gives the most conservative, largest required sample size.

faq.q: Does a bigger population always need a bigger sample?
faq.a: No. Beyond a certain size, the required sample barely changes; only small populations need the finite correction.

z-score-calculator.name: Z-Score
z-score-calculator.description: Calculate z-score and normal distribution probabilities
z-score-calculator.metaDescription: Free online z-score calculator. Standardize any raw score with mean and SD fast, no signup, and see how far it sits from the average.

steps: Enter the raw score you want to standardize.
Enter the mean and the standard deviation of the data set.
Read the z-score and what it tells you about the value's position.
guide.formula: z = (x − μ) / σ
explanation: A z-score tells you how many standard deviations a value sits above or below the mean. A positive score is above average; a negative one is below.
Z-scores let you compare values from different distributions on a common scale and identify outliers.

faq.q: What does a z-score of 0 mean?
faq.a: It means the value is exactly equal to the mean of the data set.

faq.q: Is a higher z-score always better?
faq.a: Not necessarily. It only shows distance from the mean; whether that is good depends on the context.

faq.q: How do I use z-scores to find percentiles?
faq.a: Look the z-score up in a standard normal table, or use it with the cumulative distribution to get the percentile.

p-value-calculator.name: P-Value
p-value-calculator.description: Calculate p-values for statistical hypothesis testing
p-value-calculator.metaDescription: Calculate p-values from z-scores, t-scores, chi-square, and F-statistics

steps: Enter your test statistic and degrees of freedom (or the effect size and sample size).
Select the tail type: one-tailed or two-tailed.
Read the p-value and whether the result is significant at your chosen alpha.
guide.formula: p = P(test statistic ≥ observed | H0 true)
explanation: A p-value is the probability of seeing results at least as extreme as yours if the null hypothesis were true.
A small p-value (below your alpha, often 0.05) suggests the observed effect is unlikely under the null, so you reject H0.

faq.q: Does p < 0.05 prove my theory?
faq.a: No, it only argues against the null; it is not the probability that your theory is true.

faq.q: One-tailed vs two-tailed?
faq.a: Two-tailed splits the alpha on both ends; use one-tailed only with a pre-stated direction.

faq.q: What is alpha?
faq.a: The significance threshold you set beforehand, commonly 0.05, controlling false-positive rate.

confidence-interval.name: Confidence Interval
confidence-interval.description: Calculate confidence intervals for means and proportions
confidence-interval.metaDescription: Calculate confidence intervals for population mean and proportion

steps: Enter the sample mean, standard deviation and sample size.
Select the confidence level (90%, 95% or 99%).
Read the margin of error and the lower and upper bounds of the interval.
guide.explanationTitle: What a confidence interval tells you
guide.formula: CI = mean ± z × (s / √n); margin = z × s / √n
explanation: A confidence interval gives a range that, under repeated sampling, would contain the true population parameter a set percentage of the time.
Wider intervals mean more uncertainty; larger samples or lower confidence shrink the margin of error.

faq.q: Does 95% mean 95% chance the true value is inside?
faq.a: Not exactly; it means 95% of such intervals from repeated samples would capture the truth.

faq.q: Why does n appear under a square root?
faq.a: Precision improves with √n, so you need four times the sample for half the margin.

faq.q: z vs t, which to use?
faq.a: Use t when the population standard deviation is unknown and n is small; z for large n or known sigma.

permutation-combination.name: Permutation & Combination
permutation-combination.description: Calculate permutations and combinations with and without repetition
permutation-combination.metaDescription: Calculate nPr and nCr permutations and combinations for counting problems

steps: Enter the total number of items n and how many you choose k.
Select permutations (order matters) or combinations (order does not).
Read the count and, if needed, the formula expansion.
guide.formula: permutations P(n,k) = n! / (n-k)!; combinations C(n,k) = n! / (k!(n-k)!)
explanation: Permutations count arrangements where order matters, like a podium finish; combinations count groups where order is irrelevant, like a hand of cards.
Because combinations ignore order, C(n,k) is always smaller than or equal to P(n,k) for the same n and k.

faq.q: When does order matter?
faq.a: When swapping two chosen items produces a different outcome, like rankings or passwords.

faq.q: Why is combination smaller?
faq.a: Each group of k items maps to k! permutations, so combinations divide by k!.

faq.q: What if k = n?
faq.a: Both equal 1: there is exactly one way to arrange or select all items.

ratio-calculator.name: Ratio
ratio-calculator.description: Calculate and simplify ratios, find equivalent ratios
ratio-calculator.metaDescription: Free online ratio calculator. Simplify A:B ratios, find missing values, and scale proportions fast, no signup, with clear steps.

steps: Enter the values of your ratio, such as A : B.
Add a known value for the missing side if you want to scale it.
Read the simplified ratio and any scaled equivalent instantly.
guide.formula: A : B  →  divide both by gcd(A, B) to simplify
explanation: A ratio compares two quantities and shows their relative size. Simplifying a ratio keeps the same relationship with the smallest whole numbers.
Ratios appear in recipes, maps, finance, and mixing — anywhere you need to keep one quantity proportional to another.

faq.q: How do I simplify a ratio?
faq.a: Divide both sides by their greatest common divisor so the numbers share no common factor other than 1.

faq.q: Can I scale a ratio to a known total?
faq.a: Yes. If you know one part, the calculator finds the matching other part that preserves the same proportion.

faq.q: What is a 1:1 ratio?
faq.a: It means the two quantities are equal in size; scaling one scales the other by the same amount.

binary-calculator.name: Binary
binary-calculator.description: Convert and perform operations in binary
binary-calculator.metaDescription: Convert between binary, decimal, octal, and hexadecimal number systems

steps: Enter a number in binary, decimal, or hex using the matching mode.
Select the target base you want to convert to.
Read the converted value and the bit length if relevant.
guide.formula: decimal = Σ(digit_i × base^i); binary uses digits 0–1, base 2
explanation: Binary represents numbers using only 0 and 1, with each position a power of two, which is how computers store data.
Converting to decimal sums each digit times its place value; converting from decimal repeatedly divides by the base and collects remainders.

faq.q: Why do computers use binary?
faq.a: Electronics reliably represent two states (on/off), making base 2 natural for logic gates.

faq.q: What is a bit and a byte?
faq.a: A bit is one binary digit; a byte is eight bits, the common storage unit.

faq.q: How do I convert decimal to binary?
faq.a: Repeatedly divide by 2; the remainders read bottom-up give the binary digits.

hex-calculator.name: Hexadecimal
hex-calculator.metaDescription: Convert and perform arithmetic operations in hexadecimal

steps: Enter a value in hex (using 0–9 and A–F) or another base.
Select the target base such as decimal or binary.
Read the converted result and verify digit grouping.
guide.formula: each hex digit = 4 bits; value = Σ(digit_i × 16^i)
explanation: Hexadecimal base 16 packs four binary bits into one digit, which is why it is the compact way to write memory addresses and colors like #FF8800.
Converting hex to decimal multiplies each digit by 16 raised to its position; A–F stand for ten through fifteen.

faq.q: Why use hex instead of binary?
faq.a: It is far shorter and less error-prone for long bit strings, one digit per nibble.

faq.q: What do A–F mean?
faq.a: They represent decimal 10–15 as single hex digits.

faq.q: Where is hex used daily?
faq.a: CSS colors, MAC addresses and memory dumps all use hex notation.

scientific-notation.name: Scientific Notation
scientific-notation.description: Convert to/from scientific notation and perform operations
scientific-notation.metaDescription: Free online scientific notation calculator. Convert any number to or from scientific notation fast, no signup, with mantissa, exponent and examples.

steps: Type the number you want to convert into the input field.
Choose convert to scientific notation, or from scientific notation to decimal.
Copy the formatted result with its exponent and mantissa.
guide.formula: a × 10ⁿ  where 1 ≤ |a| < 10
explanation: Scientific notation writes numbers as a coefficient between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of ten. It makes very large or very small values compact and easy to read.
It is widely used in science, engineering, and computing to handle values like the speed of light or atomic scales without long strings of zeros.

faq.q: What is the mantissa and the exponent?
faq.a: The mantissa is the coefficient (the number between 1 and 10) and the exponent is the power of ten that scales it up or down.

faq.q: How do I convert a decimal to scientific notation?
faq.a: Move the decimal point so there is one non-zero digit to its left; the number of places moved is the exponent (positive for large numbers, negative for small).

faq.q: Does the calculator handle negative numbers?
faq.a: Yes. The sign stays with the mantissa, and only the magnitude is normalized into the 1–10 range.

big-number.name: Big Number
big-number.description: Perform arithmetic on arbitrarily large integers
big-number.metaDescription: Calculate with very large numbers beyond standard calculator limits

steps: Enter one or two very large integers that exceed normal calculator limits.
Select the operation: add, subtract, multiply or compare.
Read the exact result without scientific notation rounding.
guide.formula: operations follow standard integer arithmetic on arbitrary-precision values
explanation: Normal floating-point types overflow or lose precision past about 15–16 digits, so a big-number tool uses arbitrary precision to stay exact.
This is essential for cryptography, combinatorics and any calculation where every digit must be correct.

faq.q: Why not just use scientific notation?
faq.a: Notation approximates; exact digits matter in keys, IDs and modular math.

faq.q: How many digits can it handle?
faq.a: Arbitrary precision handles thousands of digits, limited only by memory.

faq.q: Is it slower than normal math?
faq.a: Yes, big-integer routines are heavier, but necessary when precision cannot slip.

number-sequence.name: Number Sequence
number-sequence.description: Analyze and generate arithmetic, geometric, and Fibonacci sequences
number-sequence.metaDescription: Find patterns in number sequences and generate arithmetic or geometric series

steps: Enter the known terms of your sequence, separated by commas.
Run the calculator to detect the pattern (arithmetic, geometric, Fibonacci-like).
Read the next terms and the rule or formula it inferred.
guide.formula: arithmetic: a_n = a_1 + (n-1)d; geometric: a_n = a_1 × r^(n-1)
explanation: A number sequence follows a rule linking each term to its position; common families are arithmetic (constant difference) and geometric (constant ratio).
Detecting the pattern lets you predict future terms, but ambiguous short sequences can match more than one valid rule.

faq.q: What if the pattern is unclear?
faq.a: Provide more terms; short sequences often fit multiple rules.

faq.q: Arithmetic vs geometric?
faq.a: Arithmetic adds a fixed amount; geometric multiplies by a fixed factor.

faq.q: Can it handle Fibonacci?
faq.a: Yes, it can recognize recurrence rules where each term sums the previous two.

matrix-calculator.name: Matrix
matrix-calculator.description: Perform matrix operations: add, multiply, transpose, determinant
matrix-calculator.metaDescription: Calculate matrix addition, multiplication, determinant, inverse, and transpose

steps: Enter the dimensions and values of one or two matrices.
Select the operation: add, multiply, transpose, determinant or inverse.
Read the resulting matrix or scalar with each cell shown.
guide.formula: multiply: C_ij = Σ A_ik × B_kj; determinant 2x2 = ad − bc
explanation: Matrices are grids of numbers; multiplication is not element-wise but a row-by-column dot product, so dimensions must align.
Only square matrices have a determinant and inverse; a zero determinant means the matrix cannot be inverted.

faq.q: Why do matrix sizes matter?
faq.a: Multiplication needs columns of A to equal rows of B; otherwise it is undefined.

faq.q: When does an inverse not exist?
faq.a: When the determinant is zero, the matrix is singular and has no inverse.

faq.q: What is the determinant for?
faq.a: It signals invertibility and scales area/volume under the linear transform.

half-life-calculator.name: Half-Life
half-life-calculator.description: Calculate radioactive decay and remaining quantity
half-life-calculator.metaDescription: Calculate radioactive decay, remaining quantity, and carbon dating

steps: Enter the initial quantity and the half-life of the substance.
Enter the elapsed time or the remaining quantity you want to find.
Read the remaining amount and the number of half-lives passed.
explanation: Half-life is the time for a quantity to fall to half its value; radioactive and chemical decay follow this exponential law.
Because it is exponential, the amount drops by half in each equal interval, never quite reaching zero in finite time.

faq.q: What does half-life mean?
faq.a: The time needed for half of the material to decay away.

faq.q: Does it ever reach zero?
faq.a: Only asymptotically; after n half-lives 1/2^n remains.

faq.q: Is half-life only for radiation?
faq.a: No, it also describes drug clearance, cooling and many first-order processes.

distance-calculator.name: Distance
distance-calculator.description: Calculate distances between points in 2D, 3D, and on Earth
distance-calculator.metaDescription: Calculate Euclidean distance, Manhattan distance, and geographic distances

steps: Enter the coordinates or two place names, or pick two points on the map if available.
Choose the model: straight-line (haversine) or route distance.
Read the distance in your preferred units and the approximate travel time.
guide.formula: Haversine: d = 2R arcsin(√(sin²(Δφ/2) + cosφ₁cosφ₂ sin²(Δλ/2)))
explanation: The haversine formula gives the great-circle distance between two points on a sphere using their latitudes and longitudes.
Real travel distance is longer because roads and paths bend; use routing for driving or walking estimates.

faq.q: Why does the map distance differ from my GPS?
faq.a: GPS routes follow roads; the straight-line value is the shortest possible across the surface.

faq.q: What units can I use?
faq.a: Kilometres, miles, or nautical miles depending on the selector.

faq.q: Does elevation matter?
faq.a: Haversine ignores hills; for small areas the error is negligible but mountains add real distance.

random-number.name: Random Number Generator
random-number.description: Generate random numbers with various distributions
random-number.metaDescription: Generate random numbers, roll dice, and shuffle lists

steps: Set the minimum and maximum values for your range.
Choose how many numbers to generate and whether repeats are allowed.
Generate and copy the result, or re-roll for a new set.
guide.formula: Result drawn uniformly from [min, max] inclusive
explanation: Each number in the range has an equal chance; the generator seeds from the system clock so successive rolls differ.
For security-sensitive uses such as passwords or lottery draws, use a cryptographically secure generator rather than a general one.

faq.q: Can it repeat numbers?
faq.a: Toggle allow-repeats off if you need distinct values; on by default for independent draws.

faq.q: Is it truly random?
faq.a: It is pseudo-random and fine for games and samples, but not for cryptography.

faq.q: How do I pick a winner fairly?
faq.a: Set the range to entrant numbers and draw once; publish the method so the process is transparent.

tcp-throughput.name: TCP Throughput
tcp-throughput.description: Calculate theoretical TCP throughput using the Mathis formula
tcp-throughput.metaDescription: Calculate maximum TCP throughput based on MSS, RTT, and packet loss rate using the Mathis formula

steps: Enter the RTT (round-trip time) and packet loss probability.
Enter the MSS (maximum segment size, usually 1460 bytes).
Read the maximum sustainable TCP throughput for that path.
guide.formula: Throughput ≤ (MSS / RTT) × C / √(loss),  C ≈ 0.93
explanation: The Mathis equation models the throughput ceiling of a TCP connection limited by packet loss and round-trip time.
Even tiny loss (e.g., 0.1%) caps throughput dramatically on long-RTT links, which is why high-loss satellite and WAN links feel slow.

faq.q: Why does 1% loss hurt so much?
faq.a: Throughput scales with 1/√loss, so 1% loss can cut capacity to about 10% of the loss-free case.

faq.q: Does a bigger window help?
faq.a: Only up to the BDP; loss still caps the Mathis ceiling regardless of window size.

faq.q: How do I improve it?
faq.a: Reduce RTT or loss (better path, FEC, TCP variants like BBR) rather than just raising bandwidth.

bandwidth-delay-product.name: Bandwidth-Delay Product
bandwidth-delay-product.description: Calculate BDP and optimal TCP buffer size
bandwidth-delay-product.metaDescription: Calculate bandwidth-delay product and required TCP window size for optimal network performance

steps: Enter the link bandwidth and the round-trip time.
Read the bandwidth-delay product in bits and bytes.
Use it to size TCP buffers and window for long-distance links.
guide.formula: BDP = bandwidth(bits/s) × RTT(seconds)
explanation: The BDP is the amount of data that can be 'in flight' on a link at once; it sets the minimum TCP window to keep the pipe full.
A 100 Mbps link with 100 ms RTT has a BDP of about 1.25 MB, so the window must exceed that to avoid underutilization.

faq.q: Why does BDP matter for TCP?
faq.a: If the window is smaller than BDP, the sender waits for ACKs and the link never fills.

faq.q: How do I size the buffer?
faq.a: Set the TCP window and any intermediate buffers to at least the BDP.

faq.q: Does BDP grow with distance?
faq.a: Yes; RTT rises with distance, so long-haul links need much larger windows.

bb-credit-calculator.name: BB Credit Calculator
bb-credit-calculator.description: Calculate Fibre Channel BB credits for ISL links based on speed and distance
bb-credit-calculator.metaDescription: Free SAN BB credit calculator — compute buffer-to-buffer credits for Brocade FOS and Cisco MDS ISL links based on FC speed and cable distance

steps: Enter the link line rate in Gbps (e.g., 16, 32, 64).
Enter the round-trip time between the two switches in milliseconds.
Read the recommended BB_Credit buffer-to-buffer value.
guide.formula: BB_Credit ≈ RTT(ms) × lineRate(Gbps) / 10
explanation: BB_Credit is the number of buffer-to-buffer credits a Fibre Channel port advertises so the link stays full without waiting for ACKs.
Too few credits throttles long-distance links; the formula sizes credits so the in-flight data fills the pipe during one round trip.

faq.q: What happens with too few credits?
faq.a: The sender stalls waiting for ACK, leaving the link underutilized on long distances.

faq.q: Is more always better?
faq.a: Excess credits waste switch buffer memory; size to the actual RTT, not the maximum.

faq.q: Does this apply to TCP too?
faq.a: TCP uses a similar window/BDP concept; FC BB_Credit is the storage-network equivalent.

latency-converter.name: Latency Converter
latency-converter.description: Convert between ping time units (seconds, milliseconds, microseconds, nanoseconds)
latency-converter.metaDescription: Free network latency converter. Convert ping times between seconds, milliseconds, microseconds, and nanoseconds with latency category context.

steps: Enter a latency value in milliseconds, microseconds, or nanoseconds.
Choose the target unit to convert into.
Read the equivalent latency in the new unit, useful for network and storage tuning.
explanation: Latency is the time a packet or I/O request takes to travel; it is often quoted at different scales depending on the context.
Network round trips are usually milliseconds, SSD I/O is microseconds, and memory/CPU cache accesses are nanoseconds.

faq.q: Why does unit matter?
faq.a: A 10 ms vs 10 µs difference is 1000x; mixing them causes huge design errors.

faq.q: How does latency relate to speed of light?
faq.a: In fiber, light moves ~200,000 km/s, so ~5 ms one-way per 1000 km is a hard floor.

faq.q: Is lower latency always better?
faq.a: For interactivity yes, but it cannot beat physics; distance sets a minimum.

food-cost.name: Food Cost Calculator
food-cost.description: Calculate total recipe cost and cost per serving from ingredient prices
food-cost.metaDescription: Free food cost calculator. Calculate recipe cost, cost per serving, and ingredient expense breakdown for meal planning and budgeting.

steps: Enter the purchase price and package size of an ingredient.
Enter the amount the recipe actually uses.
Read the cost per serving contributed by that ingredient.
guide.formula: costUsed = purchasePrice × (amountUsed / packageSize)
explanation: Food cost links the price you pay at the store to the portion a recipe consumes, revealing the true cost of each dish.
Tracking cost per serving helps set menu prices and spot ingredients that quietly drain margin.

faq.q: Should I include waste and trim?
faq.a: Yes, factor yield percentage so peels and bones don't hide real cost.

faq.q: What is a good food cost percentage?
faq.a: Many restaurants target 28–35% of menu price, varying by concept.

faq.q: How do I price a dish?
faq.a: Divide target food-cost percentage into the total ingredient cost to get the minimum price.

recipe-scaler.name: Recipe Scaler
recipe-scaler.description: Scale recipe ingredients with smart adjustments for salt, spices, and leavening agents
recipe-scaler.metaDescription: Free recipe scaler. Double or halve recipes with intelligent scaling that adjusts seasonings and leavening for perfect results.

steps: Enter the original recipe ingredient amounts and the number of original servings.
Enter how many servings you want to make instead.
Read the scaled amounts for every ingredient.
guide.formula: scaled = originalAmount × (targetServings / originalServings)
explanation: Scaling multiplies each ingredient by the same ratio, keeping the flavor balance intact when you cook for more or fewer people.
Some steps like oven temperature stay fixed, while cooking time may need a small adjustment rather than a strict ratio.

faq.q: Does cooking time scale linearly?
faq.a: No, larger batches may need a bit more time but not in direct proportion.

faq.q: What about teaspoon amounts?
faq.a: Round sensibly; a recipe rarely needs 1.833 teaspoons precisely.

faq.q: Can I scale down to one serving?
faq.a: Yes, but very small quantities become hard to measure accurately.

nutrition-calculator.name: Nutrition Calculator
nutrition-calculator.description: Calculate calories, macros, and nutrition facts from selected foods
nutrition-calculator.metaDescription: Free nutrition calculator. Track calories, protein, carbs, fat, and other nutrients from a database of 100+ common foods.

steps: Enter the ingredients and their weights from your meal.
Enter the per-100g nutrition values or pick from a common food database.
Read total calories, protein, carbs, fat and fiber for the meal.
guide.formula: nutrient = Σ(weight_g / 100 × valuePer100g)
explanation: A nutrition calculator sums each ingredient's macros by weight, giving the totals for a homemade meal that labels never cover.
Accuracy depends on correct weights and the right database entry; branded and raw forms differ in calories per gram.

faq.q: Why weigh instead of estimate?
faq.a: Eyeballing portions can be off by 50%, distorting calorie totals.

faq.q: Do cooked and raw values differ?
faq.a: Yes, cooking changes water weight, so use the state you actually weigh.

faq.q: How accurate is the database?
faq.a: Reputable entries are close, but treat results as estimates, not medical fact.

fuel-efficiency.name: Fuel Efficiency Calculator
fuel-efficiency.description: Calculate fuel consumption in L/100km, km/L, and MPG with trip and cost estimates
fuel-efficiency.metaDescription: Free fuel efficiency calculator - L/100km, km/L, MPG conversions, trip fuel needed, and annual fuel cost estimates.

steps: Enter the distance traveled and the fuel consumed for that trip.
Enter the fuel unit and distance unit you prefer (mpg, L/100km, km/L).
Read the efficiency and the equivalent value in your chosen unit system.
guide.formula: mpg = miles / gallons; L/100km = (L × 100) / km; km/L = km / L
explanation: Fuel efficiency expresses how far a vehicle travels per unit of fuel; lower L/100km is better, while higher mpg or km/L is better.
Real-world efficiency drops in city traffic, cold weather and with aggressive acceleration, so compare under similar conditions.

faq.q: Which unit is best?
faq.a: US uses mpg, most of the world uses L/100km; pick what your region reads natively.

faq.q: Why does my car beat the label?
faq.a: Labels use standardized cycles; real driving with AC and hills differs.

faq.q: How to improve mpg?
faq.a: Keep tires inflated, reduce idling and excess weight, and drive smoothly.

vehicle-financing.name: Vehicle Financing Calculator
vehicle-financing.description: Calculate auto loan and lease payments with buy vs lease comparison (CHF/EUR)
vehicle-financing.metaDescription: Free vehicle financing calculator - auto loans, leases, and buy vs lease comparison. CHF and EUR support with Swiss VAT.

steps: Enter the vehicle price, down payment and trade-in value.
Enter the annual interest rate and loan term in months.
Read the monthly payment, total interest and total cost.
guide.formula: monthly = P × r / (1 - (1+r)^-n); r = apr/12; P = price - down - trade
explanation: Auto financing spreads the net price over a term; a larger down payment or shorter term cuts the total interest you pay.
The APR, not just the advertised monthly figure, drives lifetime cost, so compare offers by total paid including interest.

faq.q: Does a longer term lower cost?
faq.a: It lowers the monthly bill but raises total interest paid across more months.

faq.q: What is APR vs interest rate?
faq.a: APR includes fees, so it is the truer borrowing cost to compare.

faq.q: Should I pay cash instead?
faq.a: If your cash earns less than the loan APR after risk, financing can make sense.

tire-sizing.name: Tire Size Calculator
tire-sizing.description: Calculate tire dimensions, compare sizes, and check speedometer error
tire-sizing.metaDescription: Free tire size calculator - dimensions, comparison, speedometer error. Supports European metric notation (205/55R16).

steps: Enter your current tire code (e.g., 205/55R16) and the candidate size.
Enter the wheel diameter if it differs.
Read the diameter, sidewall height and speedometer error of the new size.
guide.formula: diameter = wheel + 2 × (sectionWidth × aspect / 100 / 25.4) in inches
explanation: Tire size codes encode section width, aspect ratio and rim diameter; changing them alters ride height, clearance and how fast the speedometer reads.
Stay within about 3% of the original rolling diameter to avoid ABS, gearing and odometer errors.

faq.q: What does 55 in 205/55R16 mean?
faq.a: The sidewall height is 55% of the 205 mm section width.

faq.q: Why keep diameter close to stock?
faq.a: Large deviations throw off speedometer, gearing and brake behavior.

faq.q: Can I fit a wider tire?
faq.a: Only if you have arch clearance and the rim width supports the new section.

maintenance-intervals.name: Maintenance Intervals Calculator
maintenance-intervals.description: Track vehicle service schedules and calculate next due dates with Swiss MFK reminders
maintenance-intervals.metaDescription: Free vehicle maintenance calculator - track oil changes, filters, brakes, and Swiss MFK inspection schedules. Km-based intervals.

steps: Enter current odometer reading and the manufacturer's interval (miles or km).
Enter the last service mileage and the type of service due.
Read the distance or time remaining until the next service.
guide.formula: due = lastService + interval - current; if negative, overdue by that amount
explanation: Maintenance intervals are set by distance or time, whichever comes first, so low-mileage cars still need periodic oil and inspection.
Severe duty (towing, short trips, dust) shortens intervals; following them protects resale value and reliability.

faq.q: Miles or time, which first?
faq.a: Whichever comes first; a car rarely driven still ages oil and fluids.

faq.q: What is severe duty?
faq.a: Frequent short trips, towing, extreme heat or dust that stress components faster.

faq.q: Why follow intervals strictly?
faq.a: Prevents costly failures and keeps warranty and resale intact.

unit-converter.name: Unit Converter
unit-converter.description: Convert between units of length, mass, temperature, area, volume, speed, time, data, energy, power and pressure.
unit-converter.metaDescription: Free online unit converter for length, mass, temperature, area, volume, speed, time, data, energy, power and pressure.

steps: Pick a category: length, weight, temperature, area, volume, speed, time and more.
Enter the value and choose the source and target units. If a unit is missing, switch the category first.
Read the result along with the same value expressed in other common units.
guide.explanationTitle: How unit conversion works under the hood
guide.formula: Target = value × (source factor ÷ target factor)
explanation: Each category has one international base unit: metres for length, kilograms for mass, kelvin for temperature, litres for volume. Every other unit is stored as a single factor saying how many base units it equals. A conversion first turns the input into base units, then divides by the target factor. Adding a unit means registering one factor rather than writing a rule for every pair, and it avoids the rounding drift you get from chaining factors together.

Temperature is the one category that cannot be handled by multiplication alone. Celsius and kelvin differ by an offset (K = °C + 273.15), and Celsius and Fahrenheit use a linear transform with an intercept (°F = °C × 9/5 + 32), so temperature needs its own branch. That is exactly where simple converters go wrong. Watch out too for units that share a name across regions: a US gallon is about 3.785 litres, an imperial gallon about 4.546, a gap of roughly 20%.
guide.tableTitle: Common conversions at a glance

faq.q: Why is temperature different from other units?
faq.a: Because zero is not nothing. Length and mass have absolute zeros, so a single multiplier suffices. Celsius and Fahrenheit define zero differently, with the freezing point of water at 0 and 32, so a conversion needs both a multiplier and an intercept. Multiply 25 by 1.8 without adding 32 and you get 45 instead of the correct 77 °F.

faq.q: Are US and imperial gallons the same?
faq.a: No, and the gap is significant. A US gallon is about 3.785 litres while an imperial gallon is about 4.546, roughly 20% more. The same applies to fluid ounces: about 29.57 ml in the US and 28.41 ml in the UK. Always check which system your source uses, because swapping an American recipe into British measures will be visibly off.

faq.q: How many decimal places should I keep?
faq.a: This tool keeps enough significant digits for you to round as you like. For everyday use, one decimal is plenty: height to 0.1 cm, weight to 0.1 kg. In engineering or scientific work, match the significant figures of your input data, and do not let an exact defined constant such as 2.54 become the thing that limits your precision.

faq.q: Is an ounce a weight or a volume?
faq.a: It can be either, depending on context. The avoirdupois ounce is a mass of about 28.35 grams. The fluid ounce is a volume of about 29.57 ml in the US and 28.41 ml in the UK. Recipes usually mean mass when they write oz, while drink labels mean volume, so read the abbreviation carefully.

set-calculator.name: Set Calculator
set-calculator.description: Perform set operations: union, intersection, difference, symmetric difference, cartesian product and set relations.

steps: Enter the elements of set A and set B, separated by commas.
Select the operation: union, intersection, difference or symmetric difference.
Read the resulting set listed as its unique members.
guide.formula: union A∪B, intersection A∩B, difference A−B, symmetric (A−B)∪(B−A)
explanation: A set is a collection of distinct elements; operations combine or compare sets without counting duplicates.
Union keeps everything, intersection keeps only shared items, and difference keeps what is in one but not the other.

faq.q: Why no duplicates in a set?
faq.a: By definition a set holds each element at most once; duplicates collapse.

faq.q: What is symmetric difference?
faq.a: Elements in exactly one of the two sets, excluding their shared members.

faq.q: Are sets ordered?
faq.a: No, {1,2,3} equals {3,2,1}; only membership matters.

guide.formula: bitwise: a AND b keeps bits set in both; a XOR b keeps bits set in exactly one
explanation: A programmer calculator works across binary, octal, decimal and hexadecimal and exposes bitwise logic used in low-level code.
Bitwise AND/OR/XOR and shifts manipulate individual bits, which underpins flags, masks and embedded control.

faq.q: What is a bitwise AND for?
faq.a: It masks a value, keeping only bits also set in the mask.

faq.q: Why shift instead of multiply?
faq.a: Shifting left by n bits multiplies by 2^n, often faster at the hardware level.

faq.q: What is two's complement?
faq.a: The standard way signed integers represent negatives by inverting bits and adding one.

guide.formula: Monthly surplus = extra_payment + minimums_of_paid_off_debts
explanation: The snowball method gives quick wins by clearing the smallest debt first, which can help maintain motivation.
The avalanche method minimizes total interest by attacking the highest-rate debt first, saving money mathematically.
Both methods use the same core idea: once a debt is gone, redirect its payment to the next target debt.

faq.q: Which method saves more money?
faq.a: Avalanche usually saves more interest overall, but snowball may be easier to stick with if motivation is a challenge.

faq.q: Should I stop saving while paying off debt?
faq.a: Keep a small emergency fund first; then direct extra cash toward high-interest debt before long-term investing.

income-tax.description: Calculate progressive income tax with presets or your own custom tax brackets.
income-tax.metaDescription: Free progressive income tax calculator with US, UK and custom bracket support.
income-tax.hint: One bracket per line: upper limit, rate%. Use 0 as the top limit for an open-ended bracket.

steps: Pick the region's tax brackets or a simplified schedule (e.g. US federal, etc.).
Enter gross income and deductible items (social insurance, itemized, etc.).
See tax due, effective rate, and take-home pay.
guide.explanationTitle: How income tax works: progressive brackets
guide.formula: tax = Σ(bracket income × bracket rate) − quick deduction
explanation: Most countries use progressive rates: income is split into brackets, lower parts taxed low and higher parts higher—not all at the top rate.
The gap between gross and net comes from three sources: mandatory insurance, allowances/standard deduction, and the progressive tax itself. Using deductions fully lowers the base legally.
This tool uses simplified brackets for quick planning—great for yearly estimates and 'how much more I keep after a raise'. For filing, follow local tax law.

faq.q: Why isn't all income taxed at the top rate?
faq.a: Progressive tax only applies the higher rate to the portion above each threshold; lower portions stay low, so effective rate is below the top.

faq.q: What do itemized deductions do?
faq.a: They directly reduce taxable income, lowering tax. Mortgage interest, donations, insurance—using them fully saves legally.

faq.q: Is this estimate accurate?
faq.a: It uses simplified brackets for speed. Real filing involves credits, capital gains, and special rules—consult local tax authority.
